title: The Three Dates for Deciding Ukraine’s Future
excerpt: O ver the next eight weeks , as winter envelopes Ukraine, Russia plans to use the frigid weather as a weapon
body: O ver the next eight weeks , as winter envelopes Ukraine, Russia plans to use the frigid weather as a weapon
Its arms factories have already made enough missiles and drones to take down Ukraine’s electrical grid, as well as the heating systems that millions of people rely on to stay warm
Homes far from the front will become deadly for their inhabitants as temperatures fall
In that same time frame, three events taking place thousands of miles away could determine Ukraine’s future

The first is America’s Election Day, now two weeks away; leaders in Kyiv fear that if Democrats win one or both chambers of Congress, President Trump may turn even further against them in those final weeks of full Republican control of Washington

The second is a proposed summit in mid-November in southern China, where Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to meet with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to plan how to end the war—without having a seat at the table for Ukraine
The third is the G20 summit at Trump’s Miami-area golf course, scheduled to take place in mid-December
The president has visions of standing between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as they sign a peace deal, even if he has to strong-arm Ukraine to do it, according to advisers

One Ukrainian official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to candidly discuss internal conversations, said it’s hard not to feel left out of decision making that will dictate the country’s future: “It looks like this is all happening without us.” The U.S. president, who used to brag that he could resolve the war in 24 hours, has tossed aside some sanctions on Russia and struck a deal with Putin to import diesel from Moscow, giving a boost to the Russian war machine

He and his allies have threatened Kyiv, demanding that Zelensky stop attacking Russian oil refineries or risk losing access to American intelligence, weaponry, and satellite communications that it uses to defend itself
The calendar is now Ukraine’s foe—and so, Ukrainians fear, is Donald Trump

T rump’s war in Iran has appeared to throttle Republicans’ chances in the midterms; the unending conflict, and the resulting surge in oil and gas prices, has eroded the GOP’s poll numbers and fueled Democrats’ hopes of taking both chambers of Congress
Stymied in his efforts to bring that war to a close, Trump recently shifted his focus to resolving the Ukraine conflict, in part to bring fuel prices down
But the way he’s chosen to try to do that has provided his fellow Republicans with a nasty October surprise
In a first for a U.S. president, Trump has sided with a traditional adversary, Russia, over a democracy that is not only fighting for its existence but also acting as a bulwark against a wider war

Trump’s diesel deal with Putin will have a negligible impact on American energy prices, but it’s a financial lifeline for Moscow. [ Read: Ukraine finds a new set of targets ] Trump has demanded an energy cease-fire—he even announced one earlier this month that had no basis in reality—yet has focused his ire entirely on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries
He blames those strikes for the rise in energy prices while ignoring the real culprit, Iran’s ability to defy the United States and close the Strait of Hormuz
He’s convinced himself, three people close to him have told us, that Ukraine’s attacks on the refineries are, in part, meant to undermine Republicans’ chances next month—and by extension, Trump

The president has ignored Moscow’s attacks on Ukraine’s electrical grid, and yesterday, hours after a drone strike on a public park killed six people, including two children, he downplayed its strikes on Ukraine’s cities, declaring that Russia had not “been doing much.” An image of one of the dead children, a 1-year-old killed as she sat in her stroller, was broadcast around the globe

Trump aides have threatened to withhold arms sales unless Kyiv stops targeting Russian diesel plants; this week, the administration delayed approving the transfer of missiles that Ukraine needs for its defense

Ukraine in the past week has said that it has not consistently received early warnings of attacks and no longer has full Starshield satellite access, which is impeding its ability to defend itself against Russia’s new fleet of jet-powered drones. ( The Wall Street Journal reported today that Starshield’s creator, Elon Musk, ordered the slowdown
The White House and Musk had previously denied involvement.) Some in Trump’s orbit have suggested that the United States go further and stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine
Trump’s deference to Putin has been a theme for a decade, yet this new round of kowtowing has handed Republicans another obstacle ahead of the elections

In a rare act of defiance, a handful in the party have denounced the president’s decisions, including his move to undercut a Russia-sanctions bill that he signed only a month ago in honor of its champion, the late Senator Lindsey Graham

The quick betrayal of Graham’s legacy was a blow for some of his Senate colleagues; GOP aides told us that Graham’s sudden July death cost Ukraine its most vocal champion in Trump’s inner circle, and that no one has stepped up to fill that void

Michael Froman, who worked in the Clinton and Obama administrations and is now president of the Council on Foreign Relations, told us that cutting off Kyiv from American weapons or intelligence might, in fact, prolong the war because it “would undermine Ukraine’s position at the negotiating table and make it less likely Russia would be willing to negotiate on any of the key outstanding issues.” Officials with both parties predict that the Democrats will capture the House next month; the Senate appears to be a true toss-up
Kyiv will be carefully watching the results

A Democratic win next month will, in the long run, likely help Kyiv, and some of the more hopeful members of Zelensky’s camp believe that Republican defeats could force Trump to focus more on domestic issues, resulting in him leaving Ukraine alone
But other observers on both sides of the Atlantic fear that the opposite could be true
A president without a friendly Congress tends to fall back more on foreign policy, where he needs little help from Capitol Hill
Either way, the new Congress won’t be seated until January 3, leaving Trump unchecked for two more months and perhaps motivated to wield power before his party moves into the minority

Another major national election would not be for two years—plenty of time for Trump to push Ukraine without fear of voters punishing Republicans. “He could get distracted at any time,” one outside Trump ally told us. “But right now, he’s furious at Ukraine, and he wants Zelensky gone.” T wo weeks after Election Day , Trump plans to board Air Force One bound for a series of summits in Asia
Earlier this month, Trump overruled White House aides who had counseled against him calling to wish Putin a happy birthday, warning that little good would come of it
In that conversation, Trump authorized the diesel deal, and Putin suggested something grander: a meeting of the world’s great powers to divide up the world

Putin proposed that he, Trump, and Xi hold a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen, China, in mid-November to discuss a variety of issues, including Ukraine
Trump told reporters yesterday that he is open to attending the meeting, which would be his first face-to-face encounter with Putin since their unproductive summit in Alaska last year
It is no surprise that Trump is drawn to the idea; his deference toward Putin is rivaled only by his regard for Xi, whom he hosted in lavish fashion at the White House last month

He has previously been intrigued by the idea of the three powers—China, Russia, the United States—dividing the globe into spheres of influence, although Moscow these days hardly wields the international clout of Washington or Beijing. [ Read: The deferential president ] The idea of two authoritarians and their admirer plotting to slice up sovereign nations alarmed much of the West
And how, Kyiv demanded, could Ukraine’s future be decided with no input from Ukraine? But some in Trump’s orbit have backed the idea, belittling Ukraine as a corrupt backwater with no autonomy

Putin has never viewed Ukraine as a legitimate country, and Trump has held a grudge against it since 2019, when he was impeached (for the first time) after pressuring Zelensky to dig up damaging information about Trump’s political rival Joe Biden

title: When the Public Good Is in the Hands of Big Tech
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Many people are understandably focused on the question of how AI will transform our civilization

Will it cure cancer? Will it end world hunger? Will it hack everyone’s bank accounts and incubate the next pandemic? But those who are already profiting from this technological revolution also have a more immediate concern
Their problem is—to paraphrase one of my favorite lines from Scarface —what to do with all the cash
Over the past few days, two of America’s most prominent AI leaders have offered proposals for returning some of the spoils of the AI boom to the public
On Sunday, Anthropic announced that it would set aside 5 percent of the company’s stock in a new LLC—the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund—to be spent on causes it deems to be in the public’s interest
More stock may be added as the company becomes more valuable

If the company goes public at its current projected valuation of $1.5 trillion , the fund could hold $75 billion, making it one of the largest charities on the planet. (For context, the Gates Foundation Trust had about $89 billion in it at the end of last year.) Elon Musk, a centibillionaire and a longtime skeptic of traditional philanthropy, criticized the move and tried to one-up it, writing on X that he’d be giving one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America.” According to The New York Times ’ back-of-the-napkin math, this could end up being a donation of more than $10 billion
What AI’s biggest winners decide to do with their money could have profound consequences for how Americans live their lives
The birth of modern AI may turn out to be the biggest wealth-creation event in human history, yet most Americans are feeling those effects indirectly

AI is making some people’s jobs easier and driving innovation, but it isn’t hitting everyone’s personal finances equally, and almost half of U.S. adults think the technology will widen the gap between the rich and the poor
Musk and Anthropic are now laying out two different visions for AI-driven philanthropy—raising thorny questions about the level of control that the investor class will exert over our shared future

The first and most obvious question for Anthropic: What if the company’s understanding of the “public good” doesn’t line up with the public’s wants or needs? Anthropic’s leaders, Dario and Daniela Amodei, have already committed to giving away most of their own personal wealth, and Dario has written on his blog about the kinds of philanthropy he admires
The Gates Foundation and PEPFAR, President George W
Bush’s public initiative for global AIDS relief, are both on his list
But how the firm’s leaders will actually decide to apportion these gifts remains somewhat nebulous
A press release for Anthropic’s fund lists “large donations to traditional nonprofits” and “direct distributions to specific populations” as examples of possible projects
Another stated goal is to remediate the effects of a massive, AI-driven labor-market transformation—an ironic instance of a company trying to solve a problem it helped create

As many politicians and even AI corporations themselves have argued, this tech is powerful enough, and potentially such an important part of the global economy, that the wealth it creates may merit some degree of public control

Last October, as one possible plan for reckoning with the economic consequences of AI, Anthropic floated the idea of using “sovereign wealth funds to give citizens stakes in AI revenues.” (OpenAI’s leaders have also reportedly considered giving 5 percent of the company to the government.) At least for now, though, the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund isn’t giving anyone outside of the company a stake

And the fact that it won’t be a 501(c)(3), like the Gates Foundation, means that it won’t have to deal with the kinds of mandatory financial disclosures that are meant to keep charitable organizations maximally transparent
A democratic way to approach this project would be for the government to aggressively tax the company and decide for itself how to spend the money
Not every American agrees with their government representatives’ approach to resource allocation, but at least in the public sector, the people have a voice
Although Musk’s path is also billionaire-led, it gives Americans a much more direct stake
Donald Trump clarified yesterday that Musk’s donation, if it happens, would use the country’s new child-savings accounts (known as “Trump Accounts”) as a vehicle

Rather than earmarking shares for a self-sustaining charitable foundation, Musk would be effectively cutting out the middleman, giving American children a piece of the company that houses his biggest AI bets
It would likely be a smaller total donation than Anthropic’s; one share per child may not turn out to be all that much money in the long run
And Trump Accounts aren’t a perfect dispersal mechanism ; parents can’t reject donated shares, and they can’t immediately sell them
Once account holders turn 18, though, they can spend Musk’s gift on whatever they want
Musk, like other tech billionaires , has questioned traditional modes of philanthropy
He knows that the public knows that giving can be an expression of power and control—a way to rehabilitate a donor’s image or provide political insulation for the donor and his enterprises
Musk may be getting something out of this too

If more people own a little chunk of the AI economy, will they start to become more receptive to data centers and other Big Tech interventions? The donation could also give recipients a reason to be less critical of Musk and his businesses; people with a stake in the company might be more inclined to tolerate unscrupulous behavior

Still, if he can follow through on his approach (and especially if he continues to donate AI stock, as he hinted in his post yesterday), his gift could have a real impact When SpaceX was about to go public earlier this year, my colleague Matteo Wong observed that “by weaving itself into the finances of most businesses and households in America, the AI industry is quickly making itself too big to fail.” AI is already deeply embedded in our life: in the businesses we interact with, in the pension funds and 401(k)s around which we plan our future
These massive donations, which represent a deviation from tech-industry norms, could reshape society for the better
But if the public comes to rely on Anthropic’s investments or on direct payouts from SpaceX, it’ll need to start caring even more about how well these companies perform
Public welfare needn’t be contingent on the whims of a few powerful firms; so much else already is
Elon Musk is dropping a boulder in a kiddie pool

Why is strategy so difficult? Helen Lewis on all the president’s hotties France will never be enough for the people desecrating it

title: You Can Believe Everything
excerpt: It was fitting that, just hours after the first public screenings of the Elizabeth Holmes documentary began last Thursday, Elon Musk put on a show of his own
body: It was fitting that, just hours after the first public screenings of the Elizabeth Holmes documentary began last Thursday, Elon Musk put on a show of his own
That night, in Texas, Musk unveiled the company’s new Roadster prototype, a car that would defy gravity
Tesla built what was roughly one-half of a roller-coaster loop, which the Roadster climbed before momentarily hanging upside down and then executing a controlled flip and gliding down to Earth
In another stunt, it did a barrel roll over a semi-truck
Each maneuver was powered by air thrusters that guided the car to a soft landing
But watching the clips, I could feel my brain struggling to process what I was being shown
Was this real? The car did climb vertically, flip, and land
But Musk, who has built wildly successful companies, is also famously prone to outlandish claims that don’t always pan out
I couldn’t help but wonder what, if anything, Tesla’s demonstration or Musk had elided. “This will be an actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said

He got the flying-car headlines he wanted, but will this car actually be released? There are already reasons to doubt it: The car displayed on Thursday won’t be in production until at least 2028, and it features 10 thrusters powered by 600 liters of compressed air
The flying version of the Roadster will be sold “invite-only.” Its price tag is likely to be astronomical

Rather, he’s making bold proclamations and asking people to take his pledge to deliver as an article of faith. [ Read: ] Imagine every AI agent on Earth buying the same cheap paper towels Less than 48 hours later, I found myself sitting in a crowded theater, watching the new documentary You Can See Everything , about the disgraced and convicted founder of Theranos, Elizabeth Holmes, and her husband, Billy Evans
In one scene, Holmes and Evans are hurriedly trying to court investors and research talent to build out what they refer to as Theranos 2.0
This scene is arguably the only time in the film where the duo don’t appear to be filled with existential dread

During phone calls and Zoom meetings, they spit out jargon and look earnestly excited about what they can build if they “get the band back together.” At the end of the sequence, Holmes is asked about why she’s spending her last days with her family building a company, and she responds that this is what she’s meant to be doing here on Earth
It is one of the few moments where I confidently believe her

Whatever she earnestly believes about her own guilt, it seems clear that her identity is inextricably tied to her notion that she is, in Silicon Valley parlance, a builder: a high-agency, visionary type with a remarkable risk tolerance who makes things and isn’t afraid to fail, because she has a monomaniacal obsession with pushing the bounds of what’s possible
The film, which had the biggest opening for a documentary in more than 20 years, is extremely well suited to a post-truth era
The co-directors, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, bury the audience with unreliable narration such that, when you get to the end, you feel like a participant in the film
It also left me exhilarated, slightly repulsed, and feeling as if I was going insane
In that way, the documentary replicates what it’s like to navigate the informational hall of mirrors we all inhabit
But what I found most bracing about the film—more so than the supposed unknowability of anyone or anything—is how Holmes’s act and affect do not feel like an aberration in 2026
In fact, her behavior embodies the current ethos of Silicon Valley
When she built Theranos, Holmes was a college dropout with boundless ambitions who styled herself after Steve Jobs

Jobs famously said things such as “People don’t know what they want until you show it to them,” and Holmes, like Jobs, projected the aura of a person ready to pull the future into the present by any means necessary
Jobs routinely delivered on these promises, and kept many projects secret until they were ready for the masses
Holmes did the opposite, offering a fantastical version of a product that did not exist, obscuring the actual capabilities and lying about the financials

She wasn’t alone; over time, the idea of the builder became more synonymous with a founder’s ideas, charisma, and salesmanship than with the products themselves. “I watched countless founders of hard tech companies present fraudulent products at conferences,” Nikita Bier, a tech entrepreneur who was recently Elon Musk’s head of product at X, wrote on the platform this weekend in response to the documentary. “They had fake studies with fudged numbers
Most of the adults in the room excused it as ‘faking it ‘til you make it.’” Holmes’s high-profile failure and the collapse of Theranos in 2018 didn’t kill the builder archetype
If anything, the very structure of Silicon Valley became more deeply intertwined with the builder mindset

Fake it ’til you make it (provided it isn’t outright fraud) is a necessary outcome of an industry that’s funded by venture capitalists, who often make strategic bets on projects so early in development that the products are still hypothetical
And so VCs threw unfathomable money at promising but half-baked ideas in the hopes of fabulous payouts

Failures were overlooked, even celebrated as necessary or teachable moments—honorable proof of being a “man in the arena.” In 2022, after Sam Bankman-Fried’s crypto empire was revealed to be an elaborate Ponzi scheme, the writer John Ganz argued that, in an industry built on big bets, the line between frauds and visionaries becomes difficult to suss out until everything implodes. “This is the Fyre Festival era of capitalism: outlandish promises and then a ludicrous debacle.” Much of that rush to invest has been driven by a culture progressively gripped by the fear of missing out on the next industry-shaking payout
Untold billions were poured into crypto, then NFTs, Web3, and the ill-fated metaverse

In crypto, rug-pulling scams and Ponzi schemes abounded; its boosters said things such as “Have fun staying poor.” Today we’re living through what many suggest could be an AI bubble, and the same mentality persists

Have fun staying poor has been replaced with the idea of a “permanent underclass” of people who failed to get in early and now stand to lose their economic viability, and potentially their human agency altogether

Like Theranos, crypto, and NFTs, the AI industry is defined by claims of its inevitability and its future power (to be certain, chatbots and coding agents are real and powerful in ways the other technologies were not)

In this way, AI is a faith-based technology; one’s desire to work on it, bet the success of the global economy on it, love it, or fear its End Times powers is typically predicated on what one can imagine it might become
The past eight years have warped the tech industry to the point that it can feel untethered from the constraints of reality
You can see it in headlines everywhere if you’re looking

title: France Will Never Be Enough for the People Desecrating It
excerpt: At 8 p.m. on Sunday night, President Emmanuel Macron delivered a national address to condemn the rioting and looting that convulsed France this weekend, from Br
body: At 8 p.m. on Sunday night, President Emmanuel Macron delivered a national address to condemn the rioting and looting that convulsed France this weekend, from Brittany to Perpignan

His suit and tie were black, instead of his customary navy blue, and he denounced the “seditionists from far-left fringe groups, joined by many criminals, engaged in unbridled violence in our cities.” He decried the grotesque destruction—crystallized in the viral image of a fire consuming the 19th-century wooden roof of the town hall in Limoges—and the methodical sacking of businesses. “ Rien ne le justifie, rien ne l’explique, rien ne l’excuse ,” he said : Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it

Macron acknowledged legitimate concerns about education and the cost of living, distinguished between peaceful protesters and rioters, and called for prosecutions while instructing prefects to consider banning mass gatherings
But as I was watching Macron live from New York, I called my children in Paris and heard the giddy chaos—the shouts and cheering—still vibrating through the streets below their open window
They told me that some of the stores beneath their apartment were being ransacked as the president was speaking
I had to push from my mind the appalling thought that these rioters might climb into the building’s residential upper levels

Slowly, the French authorities are starting to grasp that. “The day of disorder and violence that we have just experienced in France is one day too many,” Bruno Le Maire, a former government minister under Macron, wrote on X on Saturday, when there were roughly 2,400 arrests and 1,000 police officers and gendarmes injured, seven of them grievously
At least 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted over the weekend
Yesterday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced “localized” curfews in Paris and other cities across the country, which is a start
Today, Lecornu added that the military would be deployed this weekend, when further protests are planned

But if the government cannot restore peace quickly, then a state of emergency is the only sane option. [ Thomas Chatterton Williams: The violence sweeping France was never really about schools ] The “internal decay” besetting France, as my friend the writer Pascal Bruckner phrased it, piggybacks on other, more intelligible causes
Some of the protests began in response to genuine grievances about France’s underfunded schools and exorbitant cost of living

But they have since turned into paroxysms of disdain for healthy civic life—nothing more cerebral, nothing to do with policy. “The high-school students’ cause died on Saturday, October 17,” Bruckner wrote in Le Figaro . “It will not recover, however legitimate its original demands may have been.” An investigation published in Le Parisien yesterday concurs with Bruckner, suggesting that the recent violence is detached from the educational grievances that originally sparked the student protests

The paper reports that according to French intelligence sources, there is an alliance de circonstance between organized ultra-left militants and a larger group of young people from the banlieues encircling major urban areas, many of whom were not politically engaged and likely never expressed an interest in the movement’s original demands
Some of these insurgents sought confrontation with the state before the scheduled demonstrations even began
Others merely took the opportunity to stuff their pockets and watch their country burn
These past weeks of pandemonium have driven home for me that no society, not even a society as generous and in many ways enlightened as France’s, can make life sweet enough for angry young men
Nihilists of the kind we’ve seen flood the streets of France from coast to coast will never uphold their end of the social contract, no matter how beautifully it is drafted

This is the essence of Tocqueville’s famous paradox: As societies become more equal—and few societies strive to be more egalitarian than France, thanks to heavy taxation of the rich and a generous social safety net—any perceived or remaining inequalities become intolerable
The rioters in France are not political actors expressing the “language of the unheard,” but nihilists rebelling against the very idea of a collective national life

Whether their stated justification is racism, Islamophobia, neoliberalism, or something else, they are agents of chaos and spite, lashing out against their productive, decent neighbors, perhaps precisely because those neighbors are productive and decent
And so they burn, shatter, and humiliate the symbols of the established order
Official government estimates place the number of protesters at more than 500,000
Images from last weekend showed patrols of police forces overwhelmed by the sheer scale of the pillaging
The Macron administration was drastically underprepared for the size of the rebellion and now faces an impossible situation
Any confrontation or escalation risks providing the protesters with a martyr; if that victim comes from a marginalized demographic, the conflagration could spark a full-fledged riot. [ David A
Graham: What Trump’s comments about France say about him ] But the alternative—appeasement—is equally unacceptable
The state cannot expect its law-abiding citizens—the majority of the population, which includes the peaceful protesters—to accept its repeated failures to safeguard them and their livelihoods
A people’s ability to move freely, conduct business, and come and go from their homes through streets that are neither dangerous nor desecrated is a fundamental right

The cost of indulging the anarchists, looters, and rioters who infiltrate mass movements has fallen on the rest of France, who never consented to cover it. “We are six months away from our presidential election,” Macron reminded the country toward the end of his speech. “And so all those who are telling you today that the urgent thing is to take to the streets—to demonstrate, to create disorder—have only one goal: to damage the republic and hijack the debate.” He’s correct

But if Macron is unable to contain these forces, which seek to push the political debate into flame-scorched streets and schools and places of business, then he will be handing votes to the far-right leaders who have promised to do so.

title: Donald Trump Really Wants This Golf Course
excerpt: Sign up for Inside the Trump Presidency , a newsletter featuring coverage of the second Trump term
body: Sign up for Inside the Trump Presidency , a newsletter featuring coverage of the second Trump term
Donald Trump is treating the championship golf course he wants to build in Washington, D.C., with the gravity of an actual emergency
He has posted on Truth Social about the course at least 15 times in the past few days, including a dozen posts around 1 a.m. this morning

He wrote yesterday that work “is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY!” And the Trump administration has brought in a team of senior Justice Department lawyers, including the agency’s third in command, to defend its actions in court
Last week, when Katie Zacharia praised Trump after he fired her as press secretary, a photo she posted contained a blurred-out map on Trump’s desk of what appeared to be the golf site
It is literally at the top of Trump’s pile

A golf-course renovation is probably not the big priority you’d expect from the president just two weeks before the midterm elections, where his party will face voters who are frustrated by high prices and dislike his many vanity projects
But Trump doesn’t seem concerned that he may be risking another Reflecting Pool scandal at a high-stakes moment
On Sunday, he posted design plans for his PGA-worthy golf course

Right before a hearing yesterday, he called the federal judge presiding over a case about the golf course a “crazed lunatic” and claimed that the Interior Department could go ahead with his plan with no approval

Trump has pushed to glam up the municipal golf course in East Potomac Park near the National Mall for months, insisting in June that work would begin on “one of the Greatest Golf Courses anywhere in the World” on September 1
But starting such a project is more complicated than such a timeline would imply
The entire park is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and would be subject to extensive bureaucratic reviews

On October 10, the National Park Service, with little notice, cut down more than 400 trees, leaving the timber piled up in the middle of the course and setting off fears among locals that the president planned to blow through the usual red tape and start building
But preservationists and two golfers had sued over the pending changes earlier this year
There, the government said that the tree removals are part of a 2019 plan to restore the course to its historic state, even though the plan is seven years old and there was no rush before

Reyes, the judge in the case, has been skeptical that overgrown vegetation in the park suddenly became urgent enough to necessitate removal over a holiday weekend, especially because it coincided with Trump’s pressure over the course
Reyes insisted yesterday that this could not be a coincidence. “Both can be true,” a lawyer for the government told Reyes. “No,” Reyes replied. “Both cannot be true
We’re not dealing with quantum physics here.” Meanwhile, the design plans that Trump posted have sparked anger among the many locals who use East Potomac Park for recreation

The map appears to remove Ohio Drive, a popular running and cycling route, and to extend the golf course to the man-made island’s perimeter, removing space for picnickers and fishers; it also replaces the park’s three affordable golf courses (one 18-hole and two nine-holes) with a single, pro-level 18-hole course
Even the famous cherry-blossom trees there seem to be at risk of removal

The renovation would significantly shrink who is able to use a place Congress designated in 1897 “to be forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people.” To get to the bottom of who ordered the tree removals and for what purpose, Reyes called in several Interior and Park Service officials to testify yesterday during a hearing that stretched some seven hours

She wanted to make sense of the contradiction between the government’s position—that this was routine work, not part of any championship-golf-course plan—and Trump’s public statements. [ Read: The cutest target of Trump’s D.C. makeover ] The entire affair has been dizzying

According to Trump’s recent posts, work on the new golf course is ready to begin, the golf architect Tom Fazio has a design, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum is “very excited,” and the park will soon be closed for its big makeover
If you ask the Department of Justice, as Reyes did, Trump’s golf-course plan has not been finalized
There has been no “final agency action,” DOJ lawyers argue, meaning that according to the Administrative Procedure Act, the plan cannot yet be scrutinized in court
Fazio has no contract with the government, they said, and there are not yet official plans to close the park

Still, a DOJ lawyer asserted, when pressed by the judge, that Trump’s statements are not incorrect but can be compared to executive orders that are then interpreted by agencies in ways that are consistent with the law. (On Truth Social, Trump also added that “any variance or changes will be made, depending on site conditions, by the Experts in Parks and Recreation, whose experience and knowledge in Seawalls, Landscaping, and Design are second to none.”) If this seems confusing, that’s because it is
In a summer hearing for the case, Reyes likened the government’s stance to Schrodinger’s cat
Trump’s golf course is somehow simultaneously being built and not being built
Yesterday’s hearings captured the absurdity of the situation and the acrobatics the government seemingly must perform to defend a president who wants what he wants
Trump has focused on renovation projects with an unprecedented intensity during his second term, working to put his stamp on the nation’s capital in arch, ballroom, and sculpture-garden form
The golf course is unique, though, in that it deals not with the widely known part of Washington’s monumental landscape but with a space people use in their everyday life

The government has downplayed its golf-course efforts in court; in a filing on Sunday, DOJ lawyers likened the changes to East Potomac to redesigning “all the art exhibits in a Smithsonian Museum” and claimed that they’re relatively minor
Changing the layout of an entire historic golf course is not like changing exhibits, she said; it’s like tearing down an entire museum and building a new one

Government lawyers have tried and failed to have Reyes taken off the case, asserting in a court filing that “no reasonable observer could consider Judge Reyes sufficiently impartial to adjudicate this case.” Yesterday, she appeared especially careful, sustaining a number of objections from the government to her questions
After a more pointed exchange, she insisted that a government lawyer tell her whether she was yelling
The lawyer said that the question would be very difficult to answer

Foreshadowing the government’s arguments, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller wrote on X last week that “I missed the part of the Constitutional Convention that put federal judges in charge of golf-course maintenance.” (Reyes had not actually barred routine work on the course; rather, she’d requested notice of “major developments.”) As the hearing wound down, Reyes noted that during the final break, she had received worried texts from her mother and brother about reported death threats against her
Then she, like Miller, invoked the early days of the republic

title: Sally Rooney Is Wrong, and So Is What’s Happening to Her
excerpt: On October 14, the publisher Faber & Faber announced that it would stop selling books by the Irish novelist Sally Rooney in the United Kingdom
body: On October 14, the publisher Faber & Faber announced that it would stop selling books by the Irish novelist Sally Rooney in the United Kingdom
Rooney has declared her intention to donate her earnings to a group called Palestine Action, which was banned last year by the British government

Her publisher concluded that it could not continue to pay royalties that would end up in the hands of a registered terrorist organization. “To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher,” Faber said in a statement. “As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format.” Almost immediately, international best sellers such as Normal People and Conversations With Friends began to disappear from the shelves of British bookstores

Because of Rooney’s fame as both a “voice of her generation” and a pro-Palestinian activist, Faber’s decision provoked an outcry among advocates of the Palestinian cause, defenders of free expression, and writers and readers
Rather, their author, an Irish citizen, has decided to challenge the law of a foreign country, the United Kingdom

Britain’s 2000 Terrorism Act makes it a crime if a person “provides money or other property” and “knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism.” In this expansive language, the publisher would be on the hook along with its star author. [ Conor Friedersdorf: Europe’s free-speech problem ] By promising her royalties to Palestine Action, Rooney has forced her publisher’s hand—the key phrase in Faber’s brief statement is “in full agreement with Sally.” Faber could have tested the law in court, as courageous publishers have done in other cases, but it took a more direct course in cooperation with Rooney
She must have anticipated the storm of indignant editorials, social-media posts, and open letters that has followed the withdrawal of her books
At considerable cost to herself and her publisher, she’s using her cultural power to draw attention to the ban on Palestine Action and embarrass the British government into reversing it
This is not a story of literary censorship, but one of civil disobedience for political ends
If Rooney had earmarked her royalties for Hamas, there would be nothing more to say—she would deserve the wrath of a reasonable law
But Palestine Action isn’t Hamas; nor is it the Hilltop Youth, the movement of violent West Bank settlers

It’s a loosely organized “direct action” group of pro-Palestinian British activists whose immediate goal is to interrupt the transfer of weapons to Israel, and whose tactics amount to vandalism of property

In the summer of 2025, members broke into a Royal Air Force base in Oxfordshire and sprayed red paint on a pair of military planes, which provoked Britain’s Labour government into designating Palestine Action a terrorist organization
Other acts have been less spectacular but, in some ways, more vile
Vandals defaced and smashed the windows of a Jewish-owned investment business in an Orthodox neighborhood of North London because of its supposed ties to a weapons manufacturer
Thieves announced that they had stolen two busts of Chaim Weizmann, the first president of Israel, from the University of Manchester, where he had once been a senior lecturer in chemistry

They beheaded one, and when a pro-Israel group offered $10,000 for the busts’ return, they proposed sending an amputated ear in exchange for the money. “First bust of Weizmann is dead,” Palestine Action posted on X. “Soon, his Zionist project will be too.” (The second bust turned out to be that of a different chemist.) So far, the group has seriously harmed one flesh-and-blood human being, when a member swung a sledgehammer at a kneeling police sergeant and fractured her back during a break-in at a weapons factory
Sally Rooney’s favored activists play at being terrorists, but in fact they’re merely criminal and, by almost any definition, anti-Semitic
Britain already has laws that can deal with them
To lump Palestine Action with the Islamic State and al-Qaeda makes the word terrorism almost meaningless
Even worse, the Terrorism Act has been amended so broadly that anyone who “expresses an opinion or belief that is supportive of a proscribed organization” in a “reckless” way could get arrested

As a result, hundreds of protesters—white-haired pensioners and vicars as well as keffiyeh-muffled fellow travelers—have been detained in the past year just for holding up placards that say I Oppose Genocide

This absurdity shows up in a recent report from Britain’s Home Office: There were “3,867 arrests for terrorism-related activity in the year ending June 2026”—an increase of 1,553 percent over the previous year, before Palestine Action was banned. [ Gal Beckerman: A free-speech meltdown ] If the withdrawal from sale of Rooney’s immensely popular novels can persuade the British Parliament to amend the law and expand the permissible speech of political activists, she will have done a service for freedom of expression
But there’s no reason to believe that this is her aim, or that she even cares very much about free speech

Rooney has become a prominent advocate—the literary name and face—for the cultural boycott of Israel, including those writers and publishers who fail to meet her exacting criteria for total separation from the state where they were born and live
She refused to allow her most recent books to be translated into Hebrew until she found an Israeli publisher that supports the boycott movement
The purpose of a boycott is to ostracize its targets—to make it difficult or impossible for them to carry on a normal public existence
The only test of a commitment to free speech is the speech of people you disagree with, dislike, even despise
It’s a test that Rooney doesn’t pass and seems to have no interest in passing

Palestine Action should be undesignated as a terrorist organization; its vandals should be prosecuted under ordinary laws; its supporters should be allowed to hold up placards; Rooney’s books should be stocked, sold, and read
But she shouldn’t be turned into a martyr for a principle in which she herself has no real belief.

title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
excerpt: Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume
body: Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume
Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away

And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise.  The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail
The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies
The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water
And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down

In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying.  The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air
The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air
Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all

The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access. “Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods
Then it could go back out to dive for more.”  The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap
They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind

Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science. “One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour
It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.”

title: Here’s the tea
excerpt: When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to
body: When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story

Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773.  But after a year of research, Brown reached a different conclusion: The label was made nearly a century later
The decisive clue came when he read the Chinese text in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, as previous scholars had done

He found that the characters had been used phonetically, in slightly variant forms across contemporary sources, to represent the name of Smith, Archer & Co., a US firm that acquired Asian tea for shipment to American markets during the 1860s and 1870s

COURTESY OF MIT GLOBAL HUMANITIES Working with the Wells family, he traced the label to a relative who traveled from Michigan to California during the Gold Rush era before returning and operating a business known as the California Tea Store
Brown argues that claims for its revolutionary pedigree probably developed later, amid the centennial commemorations of the 1870s
The discovery does not make the label historically insignificant, he says

Instead, what began as an inquiry into a supposed artifact of the Boston Tea Party became a study of how ordinary objects acquire historical authority, and how historical memory itself is made. “History is never finished,” he says. “Even objects that have sat in museums for decades can reveal entirely new stories when we ask new questions.”

title: Melt it, spin it, use it again
excerpt: The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it
body: The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it

MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn.  The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typically combine spandex with polyester or nylon
Those fibers would have to be separated for recycling—a process that isn’t practical
But the MIT team found a way to create a similarly stretchy yarn from two variations of polyethylene, a material commonly used in milk jugs and grocery bags
Because they come from the same chemical family, the yarn can be melted as is

Svetlana Boriskina, who led the work as a research scientist in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, says a garment made from this material could then be spun into new yarn for a next generation of clothing

Even after 10 cycles of melting and respinning, the yarn stays as strong and flexible as conventional thread.  “Now we have something that can be knitted and woven,” Boriskina says. “That is the next stage.” Someday, the researchers hope, a polyethylene garment could be dropped in a collection bin and sent to a recycling facility, promoting a more sustainable, circular textile economy.

title: A reason to eat carbs
excerpt: A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help some people lose weight, and some research has shown that it may protect against colon cancer
body: A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help some people lose weight, and some research has shown that it may protect against colon cancer
But a new study suggests that such a ketogenic diet may also increase the risk of cancer in the small intestine
This type of diet forces the body to burn fatty acids instead of carbohydrates for fuel, producing by-products called ketone bodies
One of these, BHB, was thought to be responsible for the protective effect observed against colon cancer

Omer Yilmaz, director of the MIT Stem Cell Initiative, worked with colleagues including MIT postdocs Jessica Shay and Fangtao Chi to investigate whether the effects were similar in the small intestine

But instead, they found that mice on a ketogenic diet were more likely to develop tumors in that part of the gastrointestinal system than those on a control diet were.  Additional studies revealed that this tumor growth was driven by the way intestinal cells burn dietary fat for energy—a metabolic pathway called fatty acid oxidation

This pathway activates proteins that signal stem cells to multiply more rapidly.  “Having more stem cells means that when you injure the small intestine, it can repair itself better, but the downside is that having more active stem cells can lead to tumor formation,” Yilmaz says

Though the researchers confirmed that a ketogenic diet suppressed the development of colon tumors, their findings suggest that ketone bodies are not involved. “These molecules are essentially metabolic bystanders,” Yilmaz says
One implication is that commercial ketone supplements probably do little to either help or harm people who take them

But the deeper issue is “why the same diet has opposite consequences in two adjacent parts of the gut,” Chi says. “That is what we are working to understand next.” Whatever they discover, as Yilmaz says, “the message here is that we need to be very careful in generalizing the effects that these diets can have.”

title: Robotic therapy for stroke patients
excerpt: Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they n
body: Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need

A new approach tries to solve that problem by combining artificial intelligence and human therapy.  Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists
Drawing on what it’s learned, it gives patients just the right amount of assistance during physical rehabilitation exercises like reaching, lifting their arms, and performing tasks of daily living

The goal is “not to replace therapists, but to extend their reach,” Lachner says.  “Initial robotic experiments have already demonstrated the feasibility of this approach,” he reports. “The next phase of the project aims to develop therapist-specific models and evaluate them in a long-term clinical study with the same patients who previously received manual therapy.” Beyond that, he envisions possible applications in contact-rich industrial settings or collaborative workspaces.

title: Taking a swing at a pickleball startup
excerpt: In corporate America, Stanley Anderson ’79 says, executives often assume that their peers grew up in privileged circumstances
body: In corporate America, Stanley Anderson ’79 says, executives often assume that their peers grew up in privileged circumstances

He did not. “I spent my early years trying not to get recruited into gangs, getting shot at, watching my friends get murdered, and thinking that if I don’t leave, I will die,” says Anderson, who was raised in Chicago. “I was fortunate to survive.” But he thrived, building an impressive career at the likes of HP, Intel, and the Palo Alto Research Center
Now he is applying his management expertise as CEO of Costa Pickleball, a Las Vegas–based startup that sells high-performance paddles in decorative designs

Beyond giving customers a way to, as he says, “bring their identity to the court,” he is also betting on technology: He’s developing a quieter type of paddle he expects will provide a competitive advantage.  Succeeding in today’s pickleball market will be tough, but Anderson thinks he has what it takes, partly thanks to an important lesson he learned at MIT: “There’s nothing you can’t accomplish if you are willing to put effort into it.” Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

title: Horror films exploit how human vision works to deliver movies’ best scares
url:
<title>Horror films exploit how human vision works to deliver movies’ best scares</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767087/original/file-20261019-60-j6s7pm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=310%2C280%2C7444%2C4963&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Scary movies use visual tricks to build unease and frighten the audience.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/large-group-of-people-watching-a-suspenseful-movie-royalty-free-image/1832087647">skynesher/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><em>This article contains spoilers from popular horror movies and shows.</em></p>

<p>Imagine you’re in the movie theater watching 2018’s “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt7784604/">Hereditary</a>.” During one of the film’s most unsettling sequences, the main character, Peter, wakes up in bed disoriented. As he sits up, you hear a couple of gasps from others in the audience. The camera stays locked on Peter as he moves through his house and enters the dim living room.</p>

<p>You hear it again: more gasps. The lighting is low, a droning score builds tension, and your heart rate climbs. The people around you continue to audibly react. You haven’t seen anything scary yet, so what is everyone else responding to?</p>

<p>The camera slowly pulls back, and then you see her: Annie, Peter’s possessed mother, crouched on the ceiling in an unnatural way.</p>

<p>Watch the scene again and you might notice that Annie was in the shadows on the ceiling the whole time, following Peter through the house.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767046/original/file-20261019-50-8bj56m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Dark movie still of man in foreground from a low angle and figure up at the ceiling" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767046/original/file-20261019-50-8bj56m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767046/original/file-20261019-50-8bj56m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767046/original/file-20261019-50-8bj56m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767046/original/file-20261019-50-8bj56m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767046/original/file-20261019-50-8bj56m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=425&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767046/original/file-20261019-50-8bj56m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=425&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767046/original/file-20261019-50-8bj56m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=425&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Noticing Annie in the shadows on the ceiling might require a rewatch of ‘Hereditary.’</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://whatculture.com/film/10-scariest-horror-movie-scenes-of-all-time?page=7">A4</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>How could you have missed a human being on the ceiling, in plain view?</p>

<p>As a cognitive psychologist <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt7784604/">who studies visual perception</a>, I’ve noticed that horror movies often exploit the gap between what’s in front of your eyes and what you consciously see. Directors and cinematographers act like folk cognitive psychologists, intuitively drawing your attention exactly where it needs to be to create a scare.</p>

<h2>Directing your attention</h2>

<p>Horror movie fans have pointed out numerous examples of <a href="https://www.flickeringmyth.com/the-best-creepy-hidden-details-hanging-out-in-the-background-of-horror-movies/">spooky figures and other unnoticed details</a> in the background of scenes.</p>

<p>These blind spots exist because your visual system can’t process everything in a scene at once. You extract detailed information only from wherever your attention is directed. Anything outside the spotlight of your attention may go unnoticed, no matter how strange.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1364-6613(00)01455-8">Inattentional blindness</a> is the failure to notice something in plain view because your attention is engaged elsewhere; it’s the phenomenon behind the infamous <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vJG698U2Mvo">invisible gorilla experiment</a>, in which about half of participants busy counting basketball passes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit strolling through the middle of the game.</p>

<p>Horror leans on inattentional blindness frequently, from the ghost boy in “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1591095/">Insidious</a>” to the <a href="https://www.nme.com/features/tv-features/33-secret-ghosts-haunting-hill-house-2395122">background ghosts</a> scattered through Netflix’s “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt6763664/">The Haunting of Hill House</a>.” Something is plainly visible, though you often don’t notice it until a rewatch, and this delayed discovery can make the scene even creepier.</p>

<p>A related effect, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1364-6613(97)01080-2">change blindness</a>, is the failure to notice something changing right in front of you. The difference can be as simple as a shirt color, or something drastic like the possessed girl Janet in “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt3065204/?_ssoLoop=1">The Conjuring 2</a>” morphing into an old man during her <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z6vwaXb1e3M">interview with Ed Warren</a>. The camera stays on Ed while Janet sits slightly blurred in the background, making the transformation easy to miss until she abruptly changes back.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767054/original/file-20261019-60-kzo1c7.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Three sequential film stills of a boy reading a book in a library while a librarian stands in the background" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767054/original/file-20261019-60-kzo1c7.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767054/original/file-20261019-60-kzo1c7.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=201&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767054/original/file-20261019-60-kzo1c7.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=201&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767054/original/file-20261019-60-kzo1c7.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=201&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767054/original/file-20261019-60-kzo1c7.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=252&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767054/original/file-20261019-60-kzo1c7.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=252&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767054/original/file-20261019-60-kzo1c7.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=252&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">As the audience focuses on Ben in ‘It: Chapter One,’ the librarian slowly changes in the background as Pennywise takes over.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.reddit.com/r/ItTheMovie/comments/p9uyru/ben_hanscom_and_the_creepy_library_woman/">New Line Cinema</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Directors also steer your attention to set up a scare, pulling your focus away from something creepy, or putting it in exactly the right spot just before a <a href="https://nofilmschool.com/how-write-effective-jumpscare">jump scare</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://filmanalysis.yale.edu/editing/#eyelinematch">Eyeline match</a> is a perfect example of this strategy. In “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1457767/">The Conjuring</a>,” a girl sits up in bed, <a href="https://youtu.be/bEqmC3ens1I?si=2I4N4hCxpnJKpmc0&amp;t=95">her fearful eyes fixed upward</a>. The film cuts to reveal she’s staring at the ghost Bathsheba, crouched atop a wardrobe.</p>

<p>This editing technique works because it’s similar to something your visual system does: When someone near you looks sharply in one direction, your eyes follow automatically. Psychologists call this tendency <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.133.4.694">gaze cueing</a>, a reliable effect in attention research. Editing just mimics the real-life version to create tension, which resolves the moment you finally see what the character sees. </p>

<p>Sometimes directors do the opposite, giving your attention nothing to follow at all. The <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z4dk2ptif9I">opening sequence</a> of “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt3235888/">It Follows</a>” is a wide shot of a panicked girl running in and out of her house. With no eyeline or cut to guide you, the wide framing forces you into <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-vision-091718-015048">visual search</a>, scanning corner to corner for a danger that may not even be there yet. Will something appear in a window? Follow her out the door? The uncertainty and the search build the tension.</p>

<h2>The split between detecting and identifying</h2>

<p>Your visual field isn’t equally good at everything: Some parts of your visual system perform the initial detection, others identify what was detected. For example, <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK10848/">the fovea</a>, a tiny pit in the retina that processes the spot you’re looking directly at, contains photoreceptors called cones that process fine detail and color.</p>

<p>Beyond that central spot is your peripheral vision, dominated by photoreceptors called rods that are sensitive to motion and low light rather than detail. In a sense, your peripheral vision is set up to help you quickly answer the question “Did something just move?”</p>

<p>When there’s motion at the edge of your vision, your peripheral system <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.08.019">detects it almost instantly</a>. Your eyes make a <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK10991/">saccade</a> – a rapid eye movement – to place the fovea onto the target to identify it. That gap between detecting and identifying can create a feeling of unease because something registered, something is there, but you can’t yet say what. </p>

            <figcaption><span class="caption">Alienlike figures in ‘Nope’ pop in and out of view, pulling your attention to different parts of the screen.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Playing with peripheral vision is almost a trope in horror movies now. Think of any hallway or mirror scene where you’re focused on a character and something moves behind them, grabbing your attention before you can figure out what it is.</p>

<h2>Faces where there are none</h2>

<p>Human beings evolved to quickly detect, identify and respond to potential threats, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0703913104">such as moving animals</a>. That’s one reason vision is so sensitive to detecting movement.</p>

<p>It also explains why people are prone to <a href="https://doi.org/10.12669/pjms.346.16140">pareidolia</a>: the human bias toward detecting faces even where none exist. Have you ever seen a face in your curtains or toast? Missing a real face is potentially <a href="https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327957pspr1001_3">far costlier than perceiving a fake one</a>, so our brains likely evolved to respond even to patterns that vaguely resemble faces. </p>

<p>“<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt8772262/">Midsommar</a>” exploits pareidolia directly. As Dani is carried toward the feast after her crowning as May Queen, viewers have noticed a face in the trees. “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt9731534/">The Night House</a>” uses a similar trick, where <a href="https://youtu.be/N9RdxakUXtA?si=NW6qMEDxQ9_jsA2I&amp;t=68">ambiguous object configurations resolve into figures and faces</a> that capture your attention. The 1963 film “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0057129/">The Haunting</a>” does the same with a wall pattern during a particularly <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sog3etUwtSk">creepy scene</a>.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Directors decide what you get to see and what they leave hidden, from ambiguous shapes to sudden movements to shadowy figures in the background. They seem to understand how your visual system works, and they use this knowledge to create tension in that space between perception and recognition, as your brain tries to determine what, exactly, you’re seeing.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291955/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
