<title>US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767095/original/file-20261019-50-gztzsv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5499%2C3666&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Billionaires like Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai and Elon Musk, pictured here at President Donald Trump&#39;s 2025 inauguration, have seen their wealth soar thanks to the stock market boom and beneficial tax changes.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Trump%20Inauguration/26bfcba5785e4000b68ac1cbeec9560c/photo">Chip Somodevilla/Pool Photo via AP</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/weeks-before-the-midterms-almost-everything-is-getting-more-expensive-5b201bb5">may be affordability</a>, but <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/business/economy/wealth-boom-price-shock-midterms-rcna603013">growing anger over inequality</a> is behind the sentiment.</p>

<p>A <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2026/10/14/americans-views-of-economic-inequality-its-causes-and-who-should-fix-it/">Pew Research survey</a> released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans – including 4 in 10 Republicans – believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this.</p>

<p>This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038">has been waning</a> ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/1">sweeping legislation</a> that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs. </p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=lOhijLUAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">I’m an economist</a> who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02692171.2016.1173654">confirms the trend</a> of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674275898">policy choices</a> – including taxation and public spending – enabled this 40-year rise in inequality. </p>

<p>Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. <a href="https://itep.org/impact-of-trump-policies-on-taxes-and-consumer-costs-2026/">An analysis</a> by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%. </p>

<h2>Inequality by the numbers</h2>

<p>Recent federal data shows that <a href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/z1/dataviz/dfa/">wealth inequality continues to grow</a>. The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999.</p>

<p>These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data. </p>

<p>But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026.</p>

<p>Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories.</p>

<p>Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/us-economy-analysis-wealthy-low-income-8ba80ccc">disproportionately boosted</a> by corporate profits, which are <a href="https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A445RC1Q027SBEA">up sharply overall</a>. The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom.</p>

<h2>How taxes play a role</h2>

<p>Since President Ronald Reagan’s <a href="https://www.taxnotes.com/opinions/reagans-tax-cut-just-turned-40-and-its-still-most-important-tax-reform-world-war-ii/2021/09/03/782tf">tax cuts</a> in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become <a href="https://www.russellsage.org/publications/book/starving-beast">less and less progressive</a>, often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats. </p>

<p>The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – <a href="https://www.lse.ac.uk/research/research-for-the-world/economics/tax-cuts-for-the-wealthy-only-benefit-the-rich-debunking-trickle-down-economics">including international studies</a> – doesn’t back that up. A <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/taxes-and-growth-a-cautionary-graph/">2025 Brookings report</a> notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth.</p>

<p>Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, <a href="https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/one-big-beautiful-bill-act-tax-provisions-explorer/">which included provisions</a> making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the <a href="https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/the-2025-tax-debate-the-corporate-tax-rate-and-pass-through-deduction/">lowest corporate tax rate since 1940</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Protesters hold signs opposing President Donald Trump's tax-cut and policy bill on July 2, 2025, in Washington." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767117/original/file-20261019-70-jxzc9n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767117/original/file-20261019-70-jxzc9n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767117/original/file-20261019-70-jxzc9n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767117/original/file-20261019-70-jxzc9n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767117/original/file-20261019-70-jxzc9n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767117/original/file-20261019-70-jxzc9n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767117/original/file-20261019-70-jxzc9n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">While many voters cite affordability as a top concern, concerns over inequality have increasingly been part of this debate.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Congress%20Tax%20Cuts/707970018352472d8e510a9c577a75c4/photo">AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/the-gap-between-the-rich-and-the-very-very-rich-is-getting-wider-5f76ab6c">the composition of their wealth</a> is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from.  </p>

<p>Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of <a href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/z1/dataviz/dfa/">corporate and business ownership</a>, allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can <a href="https://budgetlab.yale.edu/research/who-paying-their-fair-share-taxes-new-analysis-and-interactive-tool">borrow against it for cash</a>, usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares. </p>

<p>By contrast, below that elite, real estate <a href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/z1/dataviz/dfa/">is a much more important component</a> of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%. </p>

<h2>The new drivers of inequality</h2>

<p>Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed.</p>

<p>One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/01/business/obamacare-enrollment-decline.html">about 5 million</a> due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs. </p>

<p>The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect <a href="https://apnews.com/article/gas-prices-incomes-spending-e68bb33d407859195cd0e383750a8d06">low- and middle-income consumers</a> but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while <a href="https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/N404RC1Q027SBEA">boosting the profits</a> of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-fuel-prices-may-go-higher-still-292853">has pushed up</a> the global price of oil.</p>

<p>Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/08/inflation-tariffs-trump-fed-consumer-goods.html">levies have inflicted a heavy hit</a> on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%. </p>

<p>This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “<a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674273559">A Brief History of Equality</a>,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294075/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%
Inequality by the numbers Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow
The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion
That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999

These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%
And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data
But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows
This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%
Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026
Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories
Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall

The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom

How taxes play a role Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive , often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats
The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – including international studies – doesn’t back that up
A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth
Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent
Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940
While many voters cite affordability as a top concern, concerns over inequality have increasingly been part of this debate
AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different
They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from

Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership , allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability
Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash , usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares
By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share
For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%
The new drivers of inequality Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played
But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed
One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse
Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs
The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point

They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil
This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil

title: How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics

<title>How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics</title>
    <content type="html"><p>With the U.S. midterms approaching, about <a href="https://gspm.gwu.edu/what-voters-think-about-ai-one-month-midterms">1 in 5 voters</a> has asked AI chatbots about elections and politics, a recent survey found.</p>

<p>But many voters may not know that governments around the world increasingly shape what chatbots can say. And because many tech companies apply <a href="https://www.trust.org/resource/the-global-impact-of-the-eu-ai-act/">the same policies</a> worldwide, the answers American voters get may be shaped by governments at home and abroad. </p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Ghtodx4AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">I’m a researcher</a> at a <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org">nonpartisan think tank</a> at Vanderbilt University, where I study <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/cf_dev/AbsByAuth.cfm?per_id=6543322">free speech policy</a>. In <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/that-violates-my-policies-ai-laws-chatbots-and-the-future-of-expression/">two reports published</a> in 2025 <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/that-violates-my-policies-ai-laws-chatbots-and-the-future-of-expression-2026-edition/">and 2026</a>, my colleagues and I worked with global legal experts to examine how governments in 12 countries and regions regulate artificial intelligence. Our research shows that they <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AI-Report-Chapter-Executive-Summary-CTF.pdf">often use existing rules</a>, such as national security or anti-state propaganda laws, rather than new AI laws to control what AI models can say.</p>

<h2>Censorship masked as safety</h2>

<p>AI can cause real harm, from <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c3ek3gvdnj3o">launching cyberattacks</a> to generating <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/jan/22/grok-ai-generated-millions-sexualised-images-in-month-research-says">sexualized images of children</a>. </p>

<p>It’s important that governments tackle these harms. But, in our assessment, some governments use legitimate concerns like these as a pretext to <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AI-Report-Chapter-Executive-Summary-CTF.pdf">control political discussion</a>, particularly chatbot responses about those in power. </p>

<p>In 2024, an Indian journalist asked Google’s Gemini chatbot whether the policies of India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/feb/26/india-confronts-google-over-gemini-ai-tools-fascist-modi-responses">were fascist</a>. Gemini responded that <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/feb/26/india-confronts-google-over-gemini-ai-tools-fascist-modi-responses">some experts say yes</a>. The <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/india/india-asks-tech-firms-seek-approval-before-releasing-unreliable-ai-tools-2024-03-04/">government reacted</a> by <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/AI-Report-India.pdf">requiring official permission</a> before “unreliable” <a href="https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/technology/government-asks-ai-platforms-seek-approval-deploying-under-trial-ai-makes-labelling-mandatory/article67912147.ece#google_vignette">AI models could be released</a>. Although authorities later <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2024/03/15/india-drops-plan-to-require-approval-for-ai-model-launches/">dropped this requirement</a>, the case shows how terms like “under-testing” or “unreliable” can be used for political purposes.</p>

<p>India is not alone. <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/AI-Report-China.pdf">China requires AI models</a> to uphold “socialist core values.”</p>

<p>And in Turkey, a court <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/turkey-blocks-xs-grok-chatbot-alleged-insults-erdogan-2025-07-09/">blocked posts by Grok</a>, the chatbot built into the social platform X, that allegedly insulted President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, founding father Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and religious values. Research by Turkish law scholar Yaman Akdeniz identifies the Turkish rulings as among the <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AI-Report-Chapter-Turkey-CTF.pdf">earliest documented cases of state censorship of chatbots</a>. </p>

<p>Vietnam shows what such content controls can mean for dissidents, including those in exile. A Vietnamese court <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AI-Report-Chapter-Vietnam-CTF.pdf">sentenced two activists</a>, who live in Germany, to 17 years each in prison in December 2025 for spreading anti-state material. Prosecutors accused them of using AI to fake voices and images of Vietnamese leaders, illustrating how <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AI-Report-Chapter-Vietnam-CTF.pdf">prosecutions can target political criticism</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767073/original/file-20261019-50-ixdxsm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An illustration of a phone screen with an AI chatbot." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767073/original/file-20261019-50-ixdxsm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767073/original/file-20261019-50-ixdxsm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767073/original/file-20261019-50-ixdxsm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767073/original/file-20261019-50-ixdxsm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767073/original/file-20261019-50-ixdxsm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767073/original/file-20261019-50-ixdxsm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767073/original/file-20261019-50-ixdxsm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The governments studied often used national security or anti-state propaganda laws to control what AI models could say.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/chatbot-artificial-intelligence-digital-concept-royalty-free-image/1494104649?phrase=ai%20elections%20political%20speech&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Vertigo3d/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Foreign rules, domestic impact</h2>

<p>Some of these government measures only affect people residing in their countries. Other statutes cross borders. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/">European Union’s AI Act</a>, adopted in 2024, requires any company offering AI tools in Europe, wherever it is based, to <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AI-Report-Chapter-EU-CTF.pdf">mark AI-generated content</a>. Anthropic, for one, <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-text-watermark">applies the marks globally</a> because it has no reliable way to <a href="https://www.fastcompany.com/91588728/anthropic-models-will-soon-inject-watermarks-identifying-ai-generated-text">apply them by region</a>. This is an example of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780190088583.001.0001">Brussels Effect</a>, in which rules adopted in the EU end up applying elsewhere.</p>

<p>European rules also affect what chatbots say about politics.</p>

<p>In August 2026, the EU <a href="https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-designates-chatgpt-reddit-roblox-under-digital-services-act">placed ChatGPT under the strictest tier of its Digital Services Act</a>, Europe’s online safety rulebook. OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, now must assess and reduce the “systemic risks” of its service, including risks to elections, such as the spread of disinformation. </p>

<p>And the Dutch Data Protection Authority tested four chatbots before the 2025 national election and found that the <a href="https://www.autoriteitpersoonsgegevens.nl/en/current/ap-warns-chatbots-give-biased-voting-advice">political middle ground</a> “virtually disappears” in their voting advice. It urged providers to “prevent their systems from being used for voting advice.”</p>

<p>These rules can be used to pressure platforms. </p>

<p>In 2024, Thierry Breton, then the EU’s top digital rules enforcer, reminded Elon Musk of his legal obligations before Musk’s live interview with then-presidential candidate Donald Trump on X, <a href="https://x.com/ThierryBreton/status/1823033048109367549">warning against the spread</a> of “harmful content.”</p>

<h2>The United States is no exception</h2>

<p>Threats to Americans’ access to information do not come only from abroad. </p>

<p>In 2025, President Trump <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/07/preventing-woke-ai-in-the-federal-government/">issued an executive order</a> on “Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government.” It requires the AI models the government buys to be “truth-seeking,” ideologically neutral and not favoring ideas such as “diversity, equity and inclusion.” </p>

<p>“Truth-seeking” may sound like an objective, neutral term, but it can mean very different things to different people. Take media reporting: The president recently <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/09/18/trump-cnn-msnow-politico-media-bans/76491a9e-b395-11f1-92c2-5c918f4a6127_story.html">banned three news outlets</a> from the White House for reporting “FICTION and LIES” and <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/01/trump-iran-war-poll-ratings-time-interview">dismissed media polls</a> as “fake.” </p>

<p>More recently, the Federal Trade Commission has suggested that AI companies that <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/ai-policy-statement_0.pdf">steer answers</a> toward undisclosed ideological or biased objectives might break consumer protection law. </p>

<p>A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 8 in 10 Americans believe Republican and Democratic voters <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/30/most-americans-say-republican-and-democratic-voters-cannot-agree-on-basic-facts/">cannot agree on basic facts</a>. In other words, as our report notes, government mandates to seek truth are often driven by ideological belief systems, particularly on political issues.</p>

<p>Meanwhile, <a href="https://www.citizen.org/article/tracker-legislation-on-deepfakes-in-elections/">dozens of states</a> have <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AI-Report-Chapter-USA-CTF.pdf">passed laws</a> restricting AI-generated political deepfakes. <a href="https://news.bloomberglaw.com/litigation/california-deepfake-parody-labels-kill-the-joke-judge-says">California</a> and <a href="https://news.bloomberglaw.com/litigation/hawaiis-deepfake-election-law-violates-free-speech-court-finds">Hawaii</a>, for example, are two states that have banned sharing deceptive AI content about candidates in the months around an election. U.S. courts have <a href="https://futurefreespeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AI-Report-Chapter-USA-CTF.pdf">blocked both of those laws</a>, citing the First Amendment.</p>

<p>What does this mean for voters? When you ask your chatbot about the elections, treat the answer as a starting point. Keep in mind that governments, both foreign and domestic, may try to influence the answer. AI responses should not replace your critical thinking at the ballot box.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294097/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Are partisan politics even changing up our accents? They just might be, y’all
url:
<title>Are partisan politics even changing up our accents? They just might be, y’all</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766784/original/file-20261016-50-2um3xt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8200%2C5466&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Increasingly, this is what conservatism looks – and sounds – like to many Americans.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/country-music-festival-live-concert-with-acoustic-royalty-free-image/1339449444?phrase=Southern%20accent%20country%20music&amp;adppopup=true">BrianAJackson, iStock/Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>With the midterms fast approaching, communicating just the right message has been top of mind on all sides of the political aisle. </p>

<p>Whether that message drives home <a href="https://www.wmtw.com/article/affordability-inflation-climbs-midterm-elections/74137545">a lack of affordability as gas, food and home prices surge</a> or <a href="https://politifact.com/article/2026/jul/09/trump-communist-democratic-socialist-chevalier/">stokes fears about the rise of communism in the American heartland</a>, Democrats and Republicans are spending a lot of time thinking about what to say.</p>

<p>But as <a href="https://www.valeriefridland.com/">a linguist who studies the impact of accents</a> on the way people are perceived, I believe how politicians and voters say what they say might be just as important as the words they use in understanding the social consequences and linguistic changes resulting from the political divides that are growing between us.</p>

<h2>Sounds of the South</h2>

<p>If there is one regional American accent that has long endured on the lips of its speakers – as well as in the minds of listeners beyond the region – it’s the Southern accent. From North Carolina through Texas and pretty much all states in between, the <a href="https://acousticstoday.org/sounding-southern-identities-expressed-through-language-irina-shport-and-wendy-herd/">so-called Southern drawl</a> has long been emblematic of <a href="https://deepsouthmag.com/2026/03/12/the-cultural-soul-of-the-southern-states/">a distinct culture found in the South</a>. </p>

<p>Yet, in the urban South, recent linguistic research finds that the drawl’s most salient features are starting to <a href="https://www.economist.com/culture/2023/10/11/young-americans-are-losing-the-southern-accent">fade on the lips of young speakers</a>. Fewer “pins” are merged with “pens,” and pronunciations such as “far” for “fire” or “say-ud” for “said” are becoming rarer.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/8DMrqucGk4k?wmode=transparent&amp;start=3" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A sociologist from the South provides an introduction to its regional accents.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>While linguists have been busy trying to understand this trend, political scientists have been measuring how different accents perform on the campaign trail. The verdict? <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1532673X18755655">Southern accented candidates</a> are generally heard as more conservative than those without a Southern accent, particularly to Democratic listeners.</p>

<p>Putting these findings from linguists and political scientists together, alongside a spate of studies examining correlations between voting patterns and vowels, hints, I believe, that the <a href="https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/political-division-united-states">increasing conservative-liberal divide in American politics</a> just might be the key to understanding what’s driving the decline of the drawl in the urban South.</p>

<h2>Out of the mouth of the South</h2>

<p>The traditional Southern accent has no shortage of stereotypes: From positive, friendly, country and down-home vibes to negative, backward, uneducated and lazy tropes, the accents of William Faulkner, Bill Clinton and the hillbilly Clampetts have weathered it all.</p>

<p>The reality, of course, is that the Southern accent is not some incorrect version of a national standard but instead a historically separate and unique dialect – or, more accurately, set of dialects. </p>

<p>As explored in <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/744046/why-we-talk-funny-by-valerie-fridland/">my recent book</a>, this dialect formed from linguistic variation that came in with colonial-era settlers from different places and stations. The incipient differences increased after the Civil War intensified hostilities and cultural differences between the North and South.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0075424211420568">association with “countryness</a>” often triggered by a Southern accent grew out of this region’s agricultural past and its related cultural folkways. But what “country” has come to mean relies largely on stereotypes about <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S095439451500006X">what a country lifestyle involves</a>. They include things like hunting, gun ownership and less socially progressive views – often arising from media portrayals of and beliefs about the South.</p>

<p>As the South has become <a href="https://www.economist.com/united-states/2023/06/12/the-south-is-fast-becoming-americas-industrial-heartland">more and more industrialized</a> over the past half-century, these social meanings associated with the accent’s use now highlight a disconnect between its new urban vibe and its older, traditional rural one.</p>

<h2>Voting and vowels</h2>

<p>As rural vs. urban ideological and political divides in the U.S. have intensified, so has using symbolic means to signal this opposition. </p>

<p>Pickup trucks emblazoned with <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2022/11/01/pickup-trucks-men-masculinity-rural-symbols/">American flags and country music have become politicized</a>. The white Southern accent, by virtue of its association with more rural traditional values, has also become <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1532673X18755655">emblematic of a conservative political identity</a> not all modern Southerners share.</p>

<p>Recent linguistic research has compared voters in the South who had strong Southern accents to those with weaker ones, mainly measured through their use of a set of <a href="https://www.unr.edu/english/people/valerie-fridland/vowels-in-america/project">unique Southern vowel pronunciations</a>, such as saying “bay-ud” for “bed” or “rawed” for “ride.”</p>

<p>It turns out that those holding more right-leaning positions and voting Republican in previous presidential elections used significantly more Southern vowels than those with more left-leaning positions who voted for Democrats. Three separate studies in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/00754242241254435">Georgia</a>, <a href="https://www.arkpsa.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/MPSR-Vol-20-2019-Husser-Eaves-Fernandez-Final.pdf">North Carolina</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.3765/exabs.v0i0.777">Tennessee</a> discovered the same relationship between degree of Southern accent and political conservatism or liberalism.</p>

<p>The takeaway from these studies is that conservatism itself is embodied in a strong Southern accent.</p>

            <figcaption><span class="caption">Dueling accents: Conservative GOP Senate candidate Rep. Mike Collins grew up in small-town Georgia; Sen. Jon Ossoff grew up in urban Atlanta.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>New sound to the urban South?</h2>

<p>The pronunciation of one’s vowels has become a barometer of how one’s beliefs and values fit within the old vs. new South.</p>

<p>Conservative ideologies and politics have become enmeshed with “country” speech and lifestyles. Young urban Southerners who don’t identify with these traits might be moving not so much away from Southern identity itself but rather specifically from this rural conservative identity it is often associated with. </p>

<p>Of course, other factors are also playing a role in the decline of the Southern accent in cities, <a href="https://apnews.com/article/migration-southern-accent-georgia-louisiana-north-carolina-1f8bfc59f869ccccaed6a87cdaa83ee8">such as heavy migration by non-Southerners to the region</a> and greater interaction with people from other dialect areas via social media.</p>

<p>Outside the South, interestingly, recent research has found a greater embrace of Southern accent features, emerging in particular among those in rural areas where traditional lifestyles and, often, more conservative views are embraced. For instance, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1215/00031283-12463431">in a small, rural town in Ohio</a>, speakers who identified themselves as more drawn to country lifestyles showed use of vowel features – such as saying “baa” for “bye” – more associated with the South.</p>

<p>So, in this circuitous and indirect way, vowels have become the latest players in partisan politics: Democratic Southerners wanting to distance themselves from the ideological and political climate associated with the rural South are moving away from its unique vowels. More “traditional” or conservative-leaning speakers continue to embrace them.</p>

<p>The real casualty in this particular battleground might be the obscuring of a larger culture, practice and community that the Southern accent has long represented for those who are automatically – and often erroneously – assigned a politicized identity just by the sound of their voice.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294125/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Are transgender sports bans really about protecting women? Survey data tells a different story

<title>Are transgender sports bans really about protecting women? Survey data tells a different story</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766275/original/file-20261014-50-9t3dle.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5543%2C3695&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Bans on transgender athletes like sprinter Sadie Schreiner, center, are often framed as protecting women.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/sadie-schreiner-who-finished-3rd-in-the-200m-race-wears-a-news-photo/2218013876">Photo by Jahi Chikwendiu/The Washington Post via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://williamsinstitute.law.ucla.edu/publications/impact-trans-sports-ban-eo/">Relatively few transgender athletes</a> participate in <a href="https://www.espn.com/espn/story/_/id/32115820/young-transgender-athletes-caught-middle-states-debates">high school</a> and <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/lgbtq/5046662-ncaa-president-transgender-athletes-college-sports/">collegiate sports</a>. Still, since 2020, <a href="https://mapresearch.org/equality-map/bans-on-transgender-youth-participation-in-sports">27 states have passed laws banning</a> them from participating in sports based on their gender identity. </p>

<p>Just weeks after his second inauguration in 2025, President Donald Trump <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/02/keeping-men-out-of-womens-sports/">signed an executive order</a> prohibiting transgender women and girls from participating in women’s sports in K-12 schools, colleges and universities that receive federal funds. Supporters of these bans often argue that they <a href="https://www.newsfromthestates.com/article/us-senate-republicans-spotlight-trans-athletes-issue-midterms-approach">protect women and girls</a> from unfair or unsafe competition. As Trump said <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/remarks-signing-executive-order-keeping-men-out-womens-sports">at the signing</a> ceremony: “we will not allow men to beat up, injure and cheat our women and our girls.” </p>

<p>WNBA star Sophie Cunningham offered a similar rationale in a <a href="https://www.espn.com/wnba/story/_/id/49306657/sophie-cunningham-finger-point-indiana-fever-wnba">July 2026 ESPN profile</a>: “I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”</p>

<p>These statements suggest that those in favor of bans are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/sipr.12099">motivated by their admiration for female athletes</a>. But are Americans with more positive views of women and women’s sports more likely to oppose transgender women competing in women’s sports?</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=OfgJBywAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">We are political scientists</a> who study <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=OsXHylAAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">public opinion</a> toward <a href="https://websites.umass.edu/lcuthbert/">transgender Americans</a>. To understand how attitudes about gender shape Americans’ views on policies that adversely affect the rights of transgender Americans, <a href="https://www.umass.edu/poll/about/reports">we asked 1,000 American adults</a> about their support for restricting the participation of transgender athletes in sports. We also asked about their feelings toward women as a group, their endorsement of sexist stereotypes and their attitudes toward policies that promote gender equity, such as <a href="https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/civil-rights-laws/title-ix-and-sex-discrimination">Title IX</a>, the law requiring schools that receive federal funding to provide women and girls with equal opportunities to participate in athletics.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A child in a purple swimsuit, seen from behind, sits at the edge of a pool beside yellow swim fins." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767071/original/file-20261019-50-840qt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767071/original/file-20261019-50-840qt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767071/original/file-20261019-50-840qt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767071/original/file-20261019-50-840qt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767071/original/file-20261019-50-840qt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767071/original/file-20261019-50-840qt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767071/original/file-20261019-50-840qt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A transgender swimmer in Utah in 2021, before the state banned trans girls from girls teams.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Transgender%20Athlete%20Lawsuit%20Utah/e898359908a44ec5850a4a506ffbe22c/photo">AP Photo/Rick Bowmer</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Sexism and support for bans</h2>

<p>Our survey found significant public opposition to transgender athletes playing on teams that match their gender identity. When asked whether they “support or oppose a bill that prohibits transgender youth from joining school-sponsored sports teams that match their gender identity,” about half of respondents supported the restriction.</p>

<p>But admiration and support for women do not translate into greater support for excluding transgender people. In fact, individuals with the most negative views of women and gender equality are the most likely to support these bans.</p>

<p>We asked respondents to rate how they feel about women on a scale from 0 to 100. Researchers have used this tool, <a href="https://doi.org/10.4135/9781446200919">known as a feeling thermometer</a>, for decades to measure how Americans feel about different groups, including people of color, gay and lesbian people and members of the opposite political party. Among respondents with the most positive views of women, 45% supported restricting transgender sports participation; among those with the most negative views of women, 58% supported restrictions.</p>

<p>We also tested whether <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2021.6">more sexist views</a> predicted support for these bans. To measure sexism, we asked respondents how much they agreed or disagreed with three statements about women: “Women seek to gain power by getting control over men,” “Women are too easily offended” and “Women exaggerate problems they have at work.” Social scientists commonly use these questions to measure “hostile sexism,” a set of stereotypes in which women are portrayed as incapable, manipulative and controlling. Among the least sexist respondents, 28% supported banning transgender people from sports matching their gender identity; among the most sexist, 79% did. </p>

<p>If admiration and support for female athletes drive support for prohibiting transgender women from participating in women’s sports, then those who favor Title IX should also favor bans. Instead, 43% of Title IX supporters favored restrictions, compared with 70% of Title IX opponents. </p>

<p>Our findings – that negative attitudes toward women and opposition to Title IX predict support for banning transgender women from sports that match their gender identity – hold even after accounting for other factors like partisanship, ideology and demographic characteristics. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Donald Trump signs a document at a desk bearing the presidential seal, surrounded by girls and young women, some in sports jerseys" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766273/original/file-20261014-50-k254ba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766273/original/file-20261014-50-k254ba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766273/original/file-20261014-50-k254ba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766273/original/file-20261014-50-k254ba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766273/original/file-20261014-50-k254ba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766273/original/file-20261014-50-k254ba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766273/original/file-20261014-50-k254ba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">President Donald Trump signs an executive order barring transgender female athletes from competing in women’s or girls’ sporting events, on Feb. 5, 2025.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/APTOPIX%20Trump%20Trans%20Athletes/3609166934034ee9ac2198e5f48496ac/photo">AP Photo/Alex Brandon</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The protection argument</h2>

<p>The debate over transgender athletes is often framed as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/sipr.12099">a matter of protecting women</a>. Our findings complicate that narrative: People with the most negative attitudes toward women – and toward policies that protect women’s sports – are the most supportive of banning transgender women from women’s sports. </p>

<p>That does not mean that everyone who supports a ban is motivated by hostility toward women. But the consistency of these findings makes it difficult to accept that protecting women is a primary reason why Americans support these restrictions.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293927/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>State takeovers of struggling Texas school districts come at a high cost, with little evidence of success</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767076/original/file-20261019-50-8jdtkw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=48%2C0%2C3886%2C2591&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Texas temporarily took over Houston&#39;s school district in 2023, following concerns about student performance. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/school-bus-is-seen-outside-condit-elementary-school-in-news-photo/1230184855?phrase=Houston%20elementary%20school%20&amp;adppopup=true">Francois Picard/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Local school boards and district administrators typically determine how public schools are run. If students are not meeting basic academic standards, though, <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/do-state-takeovers-of-school-districts-work/">state governments sometimes step in and take over</a> the day-to-day operations of entire school districts. </p>

<p>Since 1989, <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/takeover-9780190678975?cc=us&amp;lang=en&amp;">state officials have been appointed</a> to temporarily replace elected school boards and superintendents in more than 100 districts across at least 22 states. </p>

<p>Texas has used takeovers more than most. Since 2015, the state has temporarily stepped in to run eight districts. <a href="https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/84R/billtext/html/HB01842F.htm">A Texas law allows the state to take over</a> for at least two years if one or more schools within the district has poor academic performance for five consecutive years.</p>

<p>Fourteen additional districts in Texas <a href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/01/more-districts-at-risk-school-takeovers-ratings-2027/">are now at risk of a takeover</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://robinsonlab.uta.edu/">As an education professor</a> at the University of Texas at Arlington, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=EzLkaxMAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">I often evaluate educational policies and interventions</a>.</p>

<p>As part of this work, I teach a <a href="https://www.uta.edu/utamagazine/summer-2022/stories/crash-course.php">class on evaluating evidence for whether initiatives</a> live up to their claims. Based on my research, Texas taking over school districts is not always helping the students there.</p>

<h2>A decade of Texas school takeovers</h2>

<p>When a state takeover occurs, the state appoints a replacement school board, rather than holding an election. It also appoints a superintendent instead of allowing the district to hire one. </p>

<p>In October 2025, the <a href="https://tea.texas.gov/">Texas Education Agency</a> announced that it was appointing a new school board and superintendent for <a href="https://www.fwisd.org/">Fort Worth Independent School District</a>, one of the largest school districts in Texas. </p>

<p>Approximately <a href="https://fortworthreport.org/2025/08/28/these-8-charts-show-fort-worth-isds-progress-and-challenges/">82% of students</a> in this district live in poverty.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nbcdfw.com/news/local/fort-worth-isd-families-state-takeover/3936217/">Marissa Sanchez</a>, a mother with three children in Fort Worth public schools, told local station NBC 5 in October 2025, “these people that don’t know our communities, don’t know our students, what kind of representation will they bring, because we will no longer have a say in our local representative decision-making.”</p>

<p>Fort Worth’s school district had over 1,000 teachers announce their resignation during the 2025-26 school year after the announced state takeover – <a href="https://www.star-telegram.com/news/local/education/article316612636.html">up 58% from the previous year</a>. </p>

<p>It costs between US$11,000 to $20,000 for every new teacher to be recruited, trained and put in the classroom. That does not include salary, <a href="https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/2024-whats-cost-teacher-turnover">health insurance or other standard employment benefits</a>. </p>

<h2>State-run school districts skew poor, minority</h2>

<p>Only 12% of Texas schools with 80% to 100% of the student population living in poverty achieved an A performance grade <a href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/01/27/texas-school-takeover-trigger-f-grades/">during the 2024-2025 school year</a>. Meanwhile, 67% of Texas schools with a 0% to 20% poverty rate achieved an A grade, <a href="https://tea.texas.gov/about-tea/newsroom/tea-releases-2025-f-accountability-ratings-2024-ratings-now-also-available">according to the Texas Education Agency</a>. </p>

<p>Similarly, while 6% of students at schools with a majority-Black student population earned A’s, 16% of students at Hispanic-majority schools earned A’s. This compares with 35% of students at majority-white schools who received A’s. </p>

<p>At the eight Texas districts that the state has taken over – and the <a href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/01/more-districts-at-risk-school-takeovers-ratings-2027/">14 currently at risk for a takeover</a> – more than half of students who attend are eligible for free or reduced lunch. </p>

<p>And at the large districts that have been taken over, such as Houston and Fort Worth, more than 8 out of 10 students live in low-income households. A majority of students there are Black and Hispanic. </p>

<h2>Negative effect on enrollment and staffing</h2>

<p>When states take over school districts, student enrollment typically declines. Staff turnover, meanwhile, increases. </p>

<p>Teacher attrition – meaning teachers who left the profession – <a href="https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/education/hisd/article/teachers-leaving-departures-20402791.php">increased by 48%</a> during the first two years after the 2023 Houston takeover compared with the five years before. Almost 5,000 teachers left during the first year of the takeover, and another 3,300 left in the second year. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/education/hisd/article/principal-changes-2026-2027-promotions-22255831.php">Principal turnover</a> also increased dramatically in Houston, with 177 changes across 274 schools since 2024. </p>

<p>In 2023-2024, less than a year after the takeover, Houston had over 1,000 teachers not certified to teach. A year later, <a href="https://www.uh.edu/education/research/institutes-centers/iepre/reports_publications/houston_isd_takeover-2026-final-1-13-26.pdf">it had over 2,000 uncertified</a> teachers because of <a href="https://texasscorecard.com/state/texas-schools-still-allowed-to-waive-teacher-certification-requirements/">a state law</a> that allows teachers to waive the requirement that all teachers are licensed in certain cases. </p>

<p>Since the start of the takeover, about 21,000 fewer students will attend Houston public schools in 2026-2027, costing the district about <a href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/21/houston-isd-state-takeover-sustainability/">$190 million in state funding</a>. Many of these students are simply attending nearby schools that are not part of Houston Independent School District.</p>

<h2>Weighing the evidence</h2>

<p>Takeovers work, according to Texas Education Commissioner <a href="https://fortworthreport.org/2025/09/03/did-a-state-takeover-improve-other-texas-schools-these-7-charts-give-insight/">Mike Morath</a>. </p>

<p>“In every single intervention, the results were higher, or at least no worse after the board of managers was placed than before,” Morath told the Fort Worth Report in September 2025.</p>

<p>But <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228597345_When_Mayors_Lead_Urban_Schools_Toward_Developing_a_Framework_to_Assess_the_Effects_of_Mayoral_Takeover_of_Urban_Districts">national evidence</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373717705729">suggests otherwise</a>. </p>

<p>A <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/do-state-takeovers-of-school-districts-work/">recent study</a> of school takeovers nationwide concluded that takeovers, on average, do not improve student achievement. Rather, they are usually immediately disruptive to students’ reading achievement. </p>

<p>But is Texas different? </p>

<p>University of Texas at Arlington graduate students Veronica Erives, Nasja Aude, Jaclyn Foster and Cole Davis and <a href="https://tea.texas.gov/school-and-district-leaders/accountability/academic-accountability/performance-reporting/texas-academic-performance-reports">I examined</a> two Texas school districts, Shepherd and Marlin, in the spring of 2026, in forthcoming research. </p>

<h2>Uneven results after the takeover</h2>

<p>Marlin Intermediate School District, a small-town district in central Texas, has about 800 students, 99% of whom live below the poverty level. Approximately 61% of the students there are Black, 31% Hispanic and 6% white.</p>

<p>The state took over Marlin schools in 2017, following five consecutive years of failing performance grades. In 2019, Morath extended state oversight of Marlin following continued low academic performance. </p>

<p>At the time of its takeover a few years later, in 2020, Shepherd Intermediate School District served approximately 2,000 students across four rural campuses in southeast Texas, with 71% of students considered economically disadvantaged. </p>

<p>The district’s student population was approximately 56% white and 35% Hispanic, making it one of the few predominantly white districts in Texas to experience a state takeover.  </p>

<p><iframe id="1H4W0" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/1H4W0/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Third-grade reading scores in Texas school districts before and after a state takeover"></iframe></p>

<p>In both Shepherd and Marlin, teacher turnover <a href="https://www.easttexasnews.com/san-jacinto-news-times/san-jacinto-news-times/stories/sisd-moving-to-alter-compensation-plan,55717">continues to be a problem</a> years after the takeover.</p>

<p>Comparing year-to-year performance at these districts is difficult, <a href="https://tea.texas.gov/assessment-and-accountability/assessment-initiatives/staar-redesign">due to a redesign</a> of the state’s standardized testing program in the 2022–2023 school year. </p>

<p>The Texas Education Agency <a href="https://tea.texas.gov/school-and-district-leaders/accountability/academic-accountability/performance-reporting/progress-measures">explicitly notes</a> that scores from 2023 onward cannot be directly compared to older test data. </p>

<p>There is a way, however, to sort of standardize the “approach grade level” percentages by comparing them to the state percentages. This has the effect of controlling for yearly changes in the tests.</p>

<p>For Marlin, my analysis shows, the percentage of third graders who approached grade level for reading in 2016 – one year prior to the state takeover – was 41%. This compares with 73% of third graders in Texas who were reading at this level in 2016. For third grade math, Marlin’s score in 2016 was 29%, compared with 75% for the state that year. </p>

<p>By 2019, two years into the takeover, 44% of third graders were approaching their grade level for reading, and 51% of them were doing the same for math, compared with the state averages of 78% on reading and 78% on math. </p>

<p>And in 2025, while 55% of third graders in Marlin schools were reading at grade level, just 40% were completing math questions at grade level. This compared with the state’s 74% and 74% averages that year, respectively. So, slight improvement in reading, none in math, and still way below the state averages.</p>

<p>For Shepherd, 56% of third graders approached grade level for reading in 2018, one year prior to the state takeover. This compared with the state average of 77%. 
For third grade math, 57% of Shepherd students were approaching grade level, compared with the state’s 78% average in 2018. </p>

<p>By 2025, the percentages for third grade reading and math were 56 and 50, compared with the state’s 77 and 71, respectively. No gains to speak of.</p>

<p>Similar trends exist for seventh grade reading and math.</p>

<p>Our study shows little evidence of student achievement improvements to support takeovers. When weighed against the costs of declining enrollments, teacher and principal turnover, and monetary costs, one has to ask if takeovers are worth it.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/288256/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
