title: Is the US abandoning Ukraine?
excerpt: A man clears debris at the site of an air attack in Kyiv on October 19, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. | Oleksii Filippov/AFP via Getty Images This
body: A man clears debris at the site of an air attack in Kyiv on October 19, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. | Oleksii Filippov/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
You can’t quite say that President Donald Trump is “turning” on Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, because he never truly seemed to have Zelenskyy’s back

There was that time Trump panned Zelenskyy as a “modestly successful comedian.” Or that excruciating meeting where Trump and Vice President JD Vance harangued Zelenskyy for inadequately “thanking” them
But over the past week, Trump has dropped even the meager niceties he sort of faked before
On Monday, he blamed Zelenskyy for failing to end Russia’s invasion…and suggested it was time for “somebody else” to take over negotiations
Three days earlier, he delayed a package of tariffs and other sanctions designed to pressure Russia to end its four-year onslaught in Ukraine

And a week before that, Trump announced — after an apparently chummy phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin — that the US would reopen its market to Russian diesel, reversing a ban imposed shortly after the invasion.  Go a little deeper View Link All this diplomatic whiplash comes as Russia continues to bombard Ukraine with drone and missile strikes, killing hundreds of civilians in September alone and leaving hundreds of thousands of people without power
The first two weeks of October ranked among the deadliest periods for civilians in the country since 2022, according to UN monitors

But while those escalating strikes threaten both human lives and long-standing international norms around territory and sovereignty — norms that actually matter quite a lot to American security, long-term — there’s another issue that Trump is more concerned with right now: Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.  Those strikes drive up the cost of gas, and those prices are, of course, of profound concern to American voters , who are paying near- record highs for gasoline and diesel fuel (…primarily due to the war in Iran , I am obliged to note)

More than any other issue, high living costs threaten to hamstring the GOP in next month’s midterm elections.  Trump has, perhaps predictably, pursued a Russia policy that he says could ease prices at home
In addition to allowing imports of Russian diesel, Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop targeting Russian oil refineries and ramped up pressure on Zelenskyy to negotiate an end to the war

According to Ukrainian officials, that campaign has lately involved disruptions to both intelligence-sharing and the US-based satellite internet service Ukraine uses to intercept Russian attacks. (On Tuesday afternoon, Zelenskyy said intel sharing — if not satellite service — had been restored again.)  In either case, it will likely take more than arm-twisting to make the whole situation go away for good

As Vox’s Josh Keating laid out earlier this year , the US does have quite a lot of leverage over Ukraine — and Trump could very well pressure Zelenskyy to accept a peace deal with no real assurance that Russia won’t just invade again.  But we’ve all seen this movie before, as recently as 2014: Without credible guarantees, Putin could catch his breath, regroup, and return to Ukraine in a few months or years to take even more land.  The real, long-term threat there is that a stronger Russia would be even better positioned to menace the rest of Europe

And America’s power could suffer as its allies look elsewhere for less fair-weather friends.  But uh…diesel might be a bit cheaper? Thank God for small mercies, I guess.  One link for later ➨ May we suggest a truly miserable read? My colleague Marina Bolotnikova calls The Opposite of Happiness: How Bad Feelings Make and Break Us “ a bracing, useful, and even comforting lens on what it means to be alive. ” The recent book, by the noted economist George Loewenstein, examines the (necessary!) role of negative emotions in our lives and civilization…and suggests, albeit indirectly, some paths for making peace with them.  Before you go… Did you know… that Turkey is the world capital of hair transplants ? There are at least 500 clinics for that purpose in Istanbul alone, beloved by medical tourists.  Today’s trivia: What’s the currency of Poland? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the mass-market beer named after a Dutch river
The city of Amsterdam is also named for a dam on the same river.

title: The Supreme Court is about to decide whether to ban trans women from women’s sports
excerpt: Washington Interscholastic Activities Association effectively want the Supreme Court to bar trans women from women’s sports teams at high schools and universiti
body: Washington Interscholastic Activities Association effectively want the Supreme Court to bar trans women from women’s sports teams at high schools and universities. | Heather Diehl/Getty Images One of the last decade’s most consequential changes to how the Supreme Court operates is the growth of the so-called shadow docket — a process that allows the justices to decide cases unusually quickly, and often without full briefing or oral argument
Historically, the Court would typically allow contentious legal issues to percolate in the lower courts for months or even years before the justices agreed to decide one of those issues
Then they’d spend months reading briefs, hearing arguments, and debating the case amongst themselves before they finally issued an opinion

This slow process existed because the Supreme Court is the final word on many legal questions — the Court can even override Congress if it claims a law is unconstitutional — and so it should be cautious before it hands down a decision that cannot easily be displaced
A new case, which recently arrived on the Court’s shadow docket, embodies all the reasons why America’s highest Court should act carefully and slowly

Washington Interscholastic Activities Association involves a highly contentious issue — the plaintiffs in the case effectively want the Supreme Court to bar transgender women from women’s sports teams at high schools and universities, even in states that support trans inclusion in sports
It also involves an appalling sexual assault allegation
One of the plaintiffs in the case is a high school women’s team wrestler who is identified only by her initials because she is a minor
She claims that one of her wrestling opponents, who is transgender, “forcefully” penetrated the plaintiff’s vagina with her fingers during a match
As a memo from the local prosecutor’s office points out, if these allegations are true then K.M.K. is the victim of a very serious crime — rape in the third degree
The prosecutor’s office, however, decided not to prosecute because it concluded that it could not prove that a sex crime was committed beyond a reasonable doubt

Among other things, prosecutors spoke to the referee who officiated the match, and he said that “nothing stood out to him during the match” and that “after watching the video of the match, he could not say that the suspect’s hand placement was ‘anything out of the ordinary.’” The school district, meanwhile, says that it has reviewed video of the match, interviewed both competitors, and that its investigation into the allegation is “ still ongoing .” K.M.K. , in other words, is exactly the sort of case that the justices should step away from, sending it back down to the lower courts to gather more information and to fully think through the difficult legal issues presented by the case

Setting aside the horrifying allegations against her one-time opponent, K.M.K.’s lawyers — most of whom work for a Christian right law firm , the Alliance Defending Freedom (ADF) — make novel legal arguments that ask the Court to make broad pronouncements that go far beyond its previous precedents.  One of their arguments, if taken seriously by the justices, could potentially make it impossible for any school athletes, whether cis or trans, to participate in competitive sports of any kind
There is a very real risk, in other words, that the Supreme Court will, if it moves too quickly in this case, harm millions of school athletes throughout the country

The factual question of whether a particular wrestler committed a crime is separate from the legal question of whether federal law strips states of their authority over trans participation in women’s sports
And this legal question deserves more deliberation than the Court can give it if it decides this case on the shadow docket
So what are the actual legal issues in K.M.K. ? In West Virginia v

B.P.J. (2026), the Supreme Court warned that judges should not be given the power to decide which athletes may compete on a women’s sports team. “The legislatures and the schools are better equipped — and under the Constitution, are the more appropriate entities,” Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote for his Court, “to assess the competing medical and scientific considerations and draw appropriate lines.” B.P.J. , of course, was a loss for transgender rights
The Court rejected a constitutional challenge to state laws that forbid trans women from playing on school sports teams within that state
But the legal question in B.P.J. was whether laws barring trans women from women’s sports are allowed — a question that the Court’s Republican majority answered in the affirmative
A victory for the plaintiffs in K.M.K. , by contrast, would likely establish that no state may permit trans women to compete on women’s sports teams, regardless of what the people of that state want
This Court is often skeptical of claims by trans rights advocates , and it almost always resolves disputes between cultural liberals and religious conservatives in favor of the religious right
That said, this Court has thus far respected states’ rights on another contentious issue that is a high priority for the religious right: abortion
Although the Court’s Republican majority overruled Roe v

Wade and eliminated the constitutional right to an abortion, it has rejected some attempts to restrict abortion in blue states — including by repeatedly ruling against litigants who seek to ban the abortion medication mifepristone

So it is, at least, possible that this Court will follow a similar path in K.M.K. and conclude that the question of which team trans women should play on should be answered by the states and not the Supreme Court
Broadly speaking, ADF raises two legal arguments against Washington state’s policy allowing trans women to play on women’s sports teams
It claims that Title IX , a federal law that bars “sex” discrimination by most schools, implicitly requires those schools to have sports teams that only cisgender women may play on
It also claims that the Court’s recent decision in Mirabelli v

Bonta (2026), which requires public schools to out trans students to their parents even if the students wish to keep their gender identity secret, also requires those schools to exclude trans women from women’s sports
There’s no reason for the Supreme Court to decide either of these questions now, however
As Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in Lux v

Rodrigues (2010), when a party that lost in the lower courts seeks an injunction from a Supreme Court justice before their case is fully litigated in those lower courts, they must demonstrate that “the legal rights at issue are ‘indisputably clear.’” This rule, like many old rules disfavoring shadow docket decisions, exists to prevent the justices from rushing into a decision that may later prove unwise
There is no plausible argument that Title IX “indisputably” bars trans women from women’s sports

That’s because, just a few months ago in B.P.J. , the Court held that it was not deciding the question of “whether, under Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause, schools may allow biological males who identify as female to participate on girls’ and women’s sports teams.” So that’s a recent Supreme Court precedent holding that the answer to this legal question remains open
Mirabelli , meanwhile, is an unusually thinly reasoned decision

The Court’s Republican majority held that schools must out trans students because of a judicially created doctrine saying that parents have “ primary authority with respect to ‘the upbringing and education of children.’ ” But the Court’s analysis of this issue was just a single paragraph long, it relied on the most malleable doctrine in all of US constitutional law , and it had nothing to say about sports.  Moreover, as the school district points out in its brief, the Court has never held that a parent’s right to direct the upbringing of their child includes a right to dictate which rules will be used by school sports teams
If such a right existed, a parent might insist that a school bar players of a particular race
Or they might demand that their child be allowed to play football without being tackled
Competitive team sports simply cannot exist if one player’s mother is allowed to demand changes to the rules that neither the league nor the other players support

title: Why RFK Jr.’s anti-vax agenda might make eggs more expensive this winter
excerpt: USDA workers disinfected a work crew at a Jennie-O turkey farm in Eden Valley, Minnesota, during the 2015 bird flu outbreak. | Glen Stubbe/Star Tribune via Gett
body: USDA workers disinfected a work crew at a Jennie-O turkey farm in Eden Valley, Minnesota, during the 2015 bird flu outbreak. | Glen Stubbe/Star Tribune via Getty Images If egg prices surge this winter, one of the main drivers will likely be H5N1, or bird flu

Since 2022, it’s decimated the US poultry industry, resulting in the deaths of over 160 million egg-laying hens .   And when there are fewer hens, there are fewer eggs, which leads to shortages and price hikes

This happened in early 2023 when avian flu was circulating: Egg prices increased by 65 percent compared to a few months prior, and in 2025, it happened again, reaching a national average of more than $6 per dozen. (There’s also some evidence, per a Justice Department investigation, that suggests major egg companies may have colluded to raise prices , too.) We have the tools to slow the spread of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) without such high mortality, though; the United States has several effective bird flu vaccines , and egg (and turkey) producers want to use them on their birds
Last year, it seemed like they soon might be able to

In early 2025, the Trump administration announced that it would begin formulating a plan for potential vaccination by engaging with trade partners, state veterinarians, farmers, and other stakeholders
But according to reporting in Politico last week, that plan is now stalled
Why? Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F
Kennedy Jr. and his anti-vaccine agenda appear partly to blame

US Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins “pulled back on an internal USDA strategy for vaccinating poultry and egg-laying hens,” according to Politico, because she was “concerned about whether it would clash with [RFK Jr.’s] anti-vaccine views.” The pause, according to the story, “went against the counsel of expert agency staff.” The USDA didn’t respond to detailed questions for this story. “USDA has been fully committed to providing the most robust response to battling HPAI,” a spokesperson wrote over email.  Kennedy oversees the Food and Drug Administration, which has some jurisdiction over what happens on farms, though the USDA manages disease outbreaks
But he and his “Make America Healthy Again” movement apparently have enough political influence to sway how the agriculture department manages this multiyear outbreak — the largest in US history

It is risky for the birds, and consumers, and could mean that we’re going to continue to fight this devastating disease without perhaps the most effective tool to slow it down.  Why we don’t vaccinate poultry birds Just as influenza circulates in humans, H5N1 is also largely seasonal; around this time of year as ducks and geese migrate south for the winter, they shed the virus near farms
And once it infects one bird in a packed poultry barn, it quickly tears through the flock.  When birds die from the bird flu, it’s an excruciating death
However, most birds don’t die from the disease itself but rather from efforts to stop its spread
Per federal regulations, as soon as H5N1 is detected in a barn, poultry producers must cull every bird, and that culling is brutal
The predominant method entails producers sealing off the vents, which causes temperatures to rise and slowly subject the birds to death via heatstroke

Many turkey and egg producers do want to vaccinate their birds ( tens of millions of turkeys have also died due to H5N1 and resulting culling since 2022), and there are several vaccines that the USDA has deemed safe and effective
But the agency won’t allow egg and turkey producers to use them because doing so could hurt the chicken meat industry

Chickens raised for meat, known as broiler chickens, are much less likely to become infected with the virus, and the US industry exports 13.9 percent of what it produces, valued at $6.2 billion last year

And as I wrote last year : Most of the countries that import American chicken meat would pause those imports if any farmed birds in the US are vaccinated, even if no chickens raised for meat are vaccinated

The reason behind these blanket bans stems from importing countries’ concerns around the so-called “DIVA” problem, which is short for “differentiating infected from vaccinated animals.” It represents the challenge of identifying whether a poultry bird is infected with bird flu or simply has avian influenza antibodies from vaccination
In other words, the chicken meat industry has little to gain from vaccination and a lot to lose

It’s also bigger and more politically powerful than the turkey and egg sectors (two of the largest chicken meat companies — Pilgrim’s Pride and Mountaire — happen to be major Trump donors ).  Experts say that these trade problems can be solved by increasing disease surveillance and testing
In 2023, French duck farmers began vaccinating birds against H5N1

The US and Canada restricted imports for over a year, but partially lifted the restrictions after they were assured they didn’t pose a biosecurity risk.  Now, on top of resistance from the chicken meat industry, there’s Kennedy’s anti-vaccine influence.  I asked Carol Cardona , a professor at the University of Minnesota’s College of Veterinary Medicine and a proponent of vaccinating poultry birds, what she made of the Trump administration’s about-face on its vaccine plan

She quoted the historian John Barry: “When you mix politics and science, you get politics.” The US is losing the war on bird flu, and vaccines could help Given the chicken meat industry’s outsized influence on the vaccination debate, Kennedy’s position may not exert the largest push here

But it certainly hasn’t helped speed the rollout of vaccines, adding one more barrier to what many poultry veterinarians and infectious disease experts say is common sense.  HHS didn’t respond to a list of questions for this story about Kennedy’s opposition to vaccinating poultry birds. “Decisions about vaccine development and deployment must be guided by rigorous science, including evidence of safety, effectiveness against circulating strains, and the implications for animal and human health,” a spokesperson wrote, though didn’t outline any concerns over safety or effectiveness and didn’t respond to follow-up questions. “With migratory bird season here, our goals and policy have not changed: detecting, controlling, and containing HPAI in consultation with partners across the country continues each day,” a USDA spokesperson wrote to Vox.  The control and containment largely amounts to culling birds when H5N1 is detected on farms, and paying farms to improve their biosecurity by compensating them for things like repairs, rodent control, handwashing stations, and wild bird repellents.  But according to Cardona, this just isn’t working. “When biosecurity breaks over and over and over again, you have to say to yourself, there’s something wrong with the system ,” Cardona told me

She said a vaccination plan should focus on the most valuable and vulnerable species — egg-laying hens and turkeys used for breeding — and in the northern half of the US, where infection rates are much higher.  With vaccination, Cardona said, “we reduce the amount of virus in the environment, and so by doing that, we reduce the number of other species that get infected
We simply reduce, reduce, reduce.” Vaccination wouldn’t be cheap, and it could affect chicken meat exports
But chicken meat producers are “not the only stakeholders,” Cardona said, adding that regulators ought to look at the full damage that the bird flu has wrought
There’s the rise in cost to consumers who buy eggs, and the billions of taxpayer dollars spent to compensate farmers for the culled birds

Then there’s the human toll: 72 people in the US have contracted the virus since 2024, and nearly all were poultry and dairy workers; two died. (While the odds remain low, many scientists also fear bird flu could spark the next human pandemic .)  For decades, bird flu mostly just infected birds
But the toll on wildlife since 2021 has been immense, including mass die-offs of sea lions in Peru and seal pups on Antarctic islands

In 2024, the virus was first detected in dairy cattle and has now affected nearly 1,200 herds ; one study of an Ohio dairy found that each infected cow cost the farmer about $950 in lost profits.  Finally, there’s the moral cost of slowly, painfully killing hundreds of millions of egg-laying hens and turkeys
But as Cardona pointed out, bird flu, like politics, is seasonal

The Biden administration, arguably , slow-walked vaccine development and deployment until the Trump administration inherited the issue.  If egg prices do rise this winter, it likely won’t happen until well after midterms, meaning neither party will pay much of a political price for higher food costs
The costs of bird flu, instead, will be paid by consumers, vulnerable farmworkers, and most of all, the birds themselves.

excerpt: Kyla Scanlon, New York Times bestselling author and economic commentator, and Vox today announced the launch of Best of Luck , a new weekly video interview podc
body: Kyla Scanlon, New York Times bestselling author and economic commentator, and Vox today announced the launch of Best of Luck , a new weekly video interview podcast premiering October 27
Each week, Scanlon will sit down with guests who have something to teach us about how to build a meaningful career in this uncertain moment, from economists to journalists, farmers to comedians

They’ll share their most instructive detours, setbacks, and successes, and Scanlon will tie each story back to the economy that we’re all living in, with takeaways for anyone at any stage of their working life. “So much of the advice we are given about building a career still comes from an economy that doesn’t really exist anymore,” Scanlon said. “There is no one right way to build a career, especially now
The goal of this show is to ask guests how they actually did it, across the best parts, the worst parts, and the parts that were lucky
Then we put it to work! Every guest sits for a mock job interview and does an advice autopsy, and we talk about how you build your own luck

Hearing how other people found their path can help all of us make better decisions about our own.” Named to the Time 100’s Creators list and Barron’s 100 Most Influential Women in Finance, Scanlon has emerged as one of the most distinct voices making economics make sense for everyone, especially a new generation

Known for breaking down complex economic ideas and connecting them to the realities of everyday life, she coined the term “vibecession” to describe the disconnect between economic data and how people actually feel about the economy

She is the author of the New York Times bestseller In This Economy? How Money & Markets Really Work , a CNN contributor and analyst, and a monthly New York Times Opinion contributor. “At Vox, we have long been fans of Kyla’s work — her approach to explaining the economy in an accessible, approachable way really personifies Vox’s explanatory approach,” said Swati Sharma, editor-in-chief and publisher at Vox. “With this new show, we’re thrilled for her to help our audience understand how to navigate work and careers in this economy so they can live more meaningful lives.” “Kyla has a gift for translating the big, confusing picture of our economy into what it means for each of us,” said Lillian Xu, vice president of podcast business at Vox Media. “With Best of Luck , she’s doing the same for a job market that keeps changing the rules, in conversations with experts that are practical and honest about how careers really unfold today

We’re so excited to partner with her to help more people figure out what’s next.” The trailer for Best of Luck is out today, with the first episode coming on October 27 and new episodes following weekly on Tuesdays
At Vox, Best of Luck joins a stable of popular podcasts including Today, Explained , The Gray Area , and America, Actually

Vox’s shows are part of the Vox Media Podcast Network, one of the largest US podcast publishers and home to some of the most influential talent across categories, including journalist Kara Swisher and entrepreneur Scott Galloway (hosts of Pivot ), tennis champion Maria Sharapova (host of Pretty Tough ), former Manhattan US Attorney Preet Bharara (host of Stay Tuned ), basketball legend Sue Bird (host of Bird’s Eye View ), and more

Vox Media will oversee production, sales, marketing, and distribution for Best of Luck , which joins a dynamic slate of shows that shape conversations across business, culture, and beyond.  Follow Best of Luck on YouTube , Apple Podcasts , Spotify , and more
About Kyla Scanlon Kyla Scanlon is the founder of Kyla Labs

She writes about money, markets, and the systems that shape them for an audience of over 1 million people across TikTok, Instagram, Substack, and YouTube, covering the pressing issues of the day — including tariffs, artificial intelligence, energy markets, and why the traditional rungs of the economic ladder have gotten harder to climb
Her debut book, In This Economy? How Money & Markets Really Work , was a New York Times bestseller and used hand-drawn diagrams to make the machinery of the economy clear

In her newsletter, she coined the term “vibecession” to describe the disconnect between strong economic data and negative public sentiment — a concept since referenced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and taken up in research by former CEA chair Jared Bernstein
Raised in Kentucky, Scanlon studied finance, economics, and data analytics at Western Kentucky University
She started out trading options and selling cars, where she first saw how inaccessible finance had become to the people it affected most
She began making whiteboard videos and comedy skits to decode markets and economic trends for everyday audiences (and often dressed up as Jerome Powell)
She writes monthly for New York Times Opinion, has a video partnership with Foreign Policy, and is a contributor and analyst at CNN
She is also a senior fellow at the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator and a research fellow at the American Institute for Boys and Men
Scanlon was named to Barron’s 100 Most Influential Women in US Finance and the Time 100 Creators list, and has appeared on The Daily Show with Jon Stewart and The Ezra Klein Show
At work on her second book, she lives in the mountains with her dog, Piglet
About Vox Vox was launched in 2014 to address the disconnect between the widely reported facts of the day and a true understanding of why something happened
It developed a widely imitated explainer format that delivers understanding across digital platforms, newsletters, a YouTube channel with nearly 13 million subscribers, and a stable of podcasts
Under the leadership of Editor-in-Chief Swati Sharma, Vox has grown a membership programs with tens of thousands of paying subscribers
About the Vox Media Podcast Network  The Vox Media Podcast Network is one of the largest US podcast publishers and home to some of the most popular and influential shows

Reaching a monthly audience of tens of millions across audio, video, and social platforms, its podcasts spark conversations, frame issues, and define the popular zeitgeist across politics, technology, business, sports, entertainment, and more

title: Where did all the vegan restaurants go?
excerpt: My favorite restaurant, here in Madison, Wisconsin, closed this week.  It was not my favorite because it had the greatest food I’d ever had, nor the most m
body: My favorite restaurant, here in Madison, Wisconsin, closed this week.  It was not my favorite because it had the greatest food I’d ever had, nor the most memorable ambiance

But I loved the Mad Rabbit Cafe because it had become my anchor in the neighborhood — it felt like home to me and a core group of friends as surely as the century-old houses lining the surrounding city blocks

Most importantly, it was entirely vegan — a rarity in this city, which, despite its ultra-progressive politics, embraces Wisconsin’s identity as “America’s Dairyland.” It was a refuge where my most closely held values found expression
US plant-based restaurants appear to be going through a contraction, amid the tumultuous aftermath of the Covid-19 pandemic and, perhaps, an anti-plant-based cultural vibe shift

VegNews magazine reported that data from HappyCow , an app that lists vegan and vegetarian restaurants, finds the number of vegan restaurants in three of the country’s top destinations for vegan dining — New York City, Los Angeles, and Portland, Oregon — decreased by between 21 and 25 percent from 2022 to late 2024

Those cities alone make up a significant share of America’s vegan restaurants. Then, in 2025 and 2026, some of the country’s most renowned, long-running plant-based restaurants also announced that they’d shut down: Modern Love and Candle in New York City, the Vegan Joint in LA, Millennium in Oakland, a more than three-decade-old institution (though it later reopened as a leaner operation), among many others .  According to a Vegan Society report , in October 2025, HappyCow (which is like Yelp but for plant-based dining) listed 1,717 all-vegan restaurants in the US
Madison has never had anything like the vegan riches of New York or San Francisco, but even we are having our own vegan recession

When Mad Rabbit opened in early 2024, the city had four fully vegan restaurants; now, depending on how you count, one or two remain (and even the one that’s unambiguously vegan is a food-court-style stall)

I visited Mad Rabbit at its last Sunday brunch, where it served what many people have described as the best tofu scramble they’ve ever had, and a crowd-pleasing rotation of crepe specials (this month, it was mango lassi)

It’s a culinary niche that, once gone, is hard to replace in a mid-tier city like this one.  What vegan restaurants do you love — or miss? We want to hear about the plant-based restaurants that have meant something to you — whether they’re still in business or dearly missed
Did they change your mind about vegan food, make you feel at home, or become part of your routine? What do you wish you could order one more time? Email me at marina@vox.com

Mad Rabbit’s owner, Nate Anger, told me the business hadn’t been in particularly bad financial shape; it was profitable for each of the three years in which it operated, but not profitable enough to justify the punishing time commitment required to run it
Managing it had taken over his life, as it’s wont to do for many people in the food service industry. “I live here

I spend far more time here than anywhere else,” he told me in a recent interview at the restaurant. “I’ve missed my kids’ baseball game and tournaments and school band recitals.” I looked around at the oddball, DIY space he’d conjured — walls covered in houndstooth print, an Alice in Wonderland-like vortex, and art of rabbits in mischievous-looking moods, one brandishing a pair of large knives (the sort of room you wouldn’t want to encounter while stoned).  The animal rights movement has two very different emotional registers: the grief and terror of looking squarely at factory farming, and the joy of discovering how much creativity, abundance, and pleasure can exist outside it
All-vegan restaurants represent perhaps the fullest embodiment of that second feeling — like “a little heaven,” as Krupa Panchal, co-owner of Bombay Food Junkies, a vegan Indian spot in suburban St
Louis, put it to me.  Even as vegan businesses struggle to survive, plant-based options at non-vegan restaurants have become far more mainstream than they were a decade or two ago
Set against the stagnating (if not declining ) share of Americans who identify as vegan or vegetarian, that raises difficult and even paradoxical questions for the animal movement
For that reason, the mass die-off of plant-based restaurants has been much dissected and lamented in the vegan community
As I faced losing my own — a possibility I’d always feared and tried to forestall by supporting it as much as possible — the problem became much more visceral for me

I found myself thinking about why it mattered to me so much: What is lost when these places disappear, and what does that tell us about whether the plant-based movement can grow and endure? What vegan restaurants are for The vegan restaurant predates the word “vegan” itself — and so, apparently, do questions about whether they can be financially viable

More than a century ago, French anarchist Georges Butaud co-founded the Foyer Végétalien in Paris, writing in a 1923 letter that he was unsure whether it would attract a sufficient “clientèle végétalienne” to sustain itself
Why start such a business at all, when the audience for plant-based food is so vanishingly small? “I already have some positive results
A few people have become vegan since we opened,” Butaud wrote

The restaurant “is a school where we reciprocally teach one another…I have believed in the usefulness of creating it, and I will be happy if, over the months to come, the number of vegans increases.”  Many vegan restaurant proprietors today still share that ambition — to be good enough to help the movement grow.  Long before it became routine to find plant-based options on normie restaurant menus (iceberg lettuce leaves don’t count), plant-based restaurants compensated for vegans’ exclusion from mainstream cuisine

But they have also aimed to provide proof of concept of the diverse, surprising possibilities of plant-based food for a larger audience, showing that plant-based food need not be confined to marginalia.  Today, of course, restaurants are far more central to our daily lives than they were in Butaud’s time
Americans consume about a third of their calories and the majority of their food budgets outside the home, and food-serving businesses are perhaps our most important third spaces
Meanwhile, the problems associated with animal agriculture and overconsumption of animal products grow unabated in America and around the world
The US alone slaughters 10 billion land animals for meat every year, the overwhelming share of them raised in appalling conditions, and those farmed for milk and eggs endure no better
Reciting these grim facts tends not to be a very fruitful path toward making friends or convincing people that veganism can be a positive and enjoyable lifestyle

Plant-based restaurants, on the other hand, make veganism feel less like a prohibition than an invitation; hospitality rather than horror.  Anyone who has ever gone vegan knows what it’s like to incessantly be asked the well-meaning but bewildering question: “What do you eat?” (And, I get it! It’s confusing for those of us who grew up viewing food free of animal products as side salad or overcooked green beans.) Plant-based businesses have long been laboratories for answering it, developing techniques that draw richness and variety from ingredients not often treated as the main event in Western cuisines

The more than 50-year-old Moosewood Restaurant (although mostly vegetarian, not fully vegan) was an early conduit between restaurant experimentation and home cooking, its recipes spreading far beyond Ithaca, New York, through its enormously popular cookbooks

Soul Vegetarian in Atlanta, opened in 1979, developed a plant-based soul food repertoire that helped cut a path for dozens of other vegan soul restaurants across the US; the Chicago Diner, in the city long identified with stockyards and slaughterhouses, helped popularize plant-based versions of American diner and deli staples

And chef Miyoko Schinner, at her erstwhile San Francisco restaurant Now & Zen, experimented with plant-based cheeses long before launching Miyoko’s Creamery, one of the most acclaimed and influential vegan dairy companies of the past decade.  The 21st century in particular has seen a flowering of vegan restaurants serving every palate and national cuisine, in every possible aesthetic — punk, hippie, psychedelic, fussy and upscale. They still expand my mind today, showing that a lifetime wouldn’t be enough to discover all the ways we can eat without the exploitation of animals

The longtime Grasshopper restaurant in Boston, whose pan-Asian fare draws partly from Vietnamese Buddhist temple cuisine, makes mock meats that are worlds away from the rubbery substitutes that many Americans associate with the category (it closed its beloved, homey restaurant space in 2024, later reopening a stall inside a food court)
Mad Rabbit changed even this longtime vegan’s idea of what tofu could be
Chicago-based Penelope’s Vegan Taqueria makes, as far as I’m concerned, the most exceptional Mexican food — vegan or not — this side of the Rio Grande

V-Grits, a Southern comfort spot in Louisville, Kentucky (RIP, 2024), provided evidence that some of America’s most exciting plant-based food could be found far from the big coastal cities best known for it.  So why are so many of these places shuttering now?  The vegan restaurant death spiral?  Theories abound about the great dying of vegan restaurants
Some of the casualties, it must be said, just weren’t very good in the first place
The raw vegan boom of the 2000s and 2010s, for example, produced numerous establishments built around that especially unforgiving constraint — no cooking
The result was often less-than-thrilling food (which isn’t to say it’s never good!), all in service of a restriction with scant evidence of health benefits to support it

title: What should you do if your friend is in love with you?
excerpt: Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary
body: Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary
I’m honored to be subbing for Sigal Samuel while she’s out on parental leave
I’m diving into your questions as a way to help understand human nature and our choices through multiple lenses: philosophical, psychological, and beyond
Please send in any emotional, body/brain, sociological, perceptual, or other kind of life quandaries you might have
My best friend confessed his love for me one year ago and I rejected him because I was unhappily in love with another man, and I was never really physically attracted to my best friend
Over a year later, I find myself thinking about how it would be like to be in a relationship with my best friend
He is the only man who ever showed me genuine love and support, and I wonder what if I try…maybe I will fall in love with him
However, I am concerned about hurting his feelings again

Is it selfish of me wanting to try this love out because it promises security and appreciation? Dear Fanning the Flame, I can’t blame you for being curious about the common “friends to lovers” storyline

It’s often portrayed as the best kind of pairing: Two people have the foundation of their friendship plus a newfound love; the romantic relationship is like a soaring addition to an existing sturdy house.  But real life is not always like the movies, and it sounds to me like you haven’t actually had an awakening of desire for your friend
In fact, it’s the opposite: He once expressed feelings for you, and you confronted a lack of physical attraction for this person
Now you’re wondering if it would be possible for you to fall in love if you tried
I think you’d agree that your timing is suspect
After a breakup, it’s common and understandable to seek out comfort and intimacy

Still, I detect a philosophical streak in your question beyond the issue of whether or not this would simply be a rebound.  Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions

Sign up here! If your friend has always appreciated you, made you feel safe, and loves you — could that be a form of love that’s better than what you had in your last relationship? Maybe that is what love is

Is it? Over a long night of drinking some 2,400 years ago, one group of thinkers allegedly debated the true nature of love, as Greek philosopher Plato describes in The Symposium .  Aristophanes, a playwright, tells a story that most closely aligns with the love we see in the rom-coms of today
He said that humans used to be larger creatures with four arms and four legs
After annoying the gods, Zeus cuts all the humans in half, creating the two-limbed bodies we have today
The result is that people wander the world looking for the one person who used to literally complete them

If you followed Aristophanes’s fable, you shouldn’t try to be with your friend unless you felt that deep longing that one has when meeting their other half.  The rest of the dinner party companions have more circumspect ideas
Phaedrus, a Greek aristocrat, thought that true love inspired people to become the best possible version of themselves
Pausanias, a military man, thought that love driven only by attraction to someone’s body was “vulgar love”, and that “noble love” was the love of someone’s values
Eryximachus, a doctor, asserts that love is also about moderation, and it needs order, much in the way the natural world does
Finally, Socrates says that even if you start out with physical infatuation, you can eventually transcend that and end up loving wisdom itself, the highest form of love
As I read it, the men are grappling with how to make love make sense, while acknowledging that it can make us lustful and impulsive
Shouldn’t its best manifestations instead be practical and virtuous?    You could easily justify trying to date your friend with these theories that try to wrangle and tame love
For example, if your friend inspires you to be the best version of yourself, you could decide that’s enough to go for it

You could also decide that because you admire your friend’s character, and not his body, that’s a noble love, and better than the vulgar love of attraction.  German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer wrote in his 19th-century essay “ The Metaphysics of Sexual Love ” that he distrusted the feeling of being desperately in love
He considered romantic love to be a biological drive disguised as a real emotion — one whose goal is to trick us into procreating

You could even see your lack of attraction as an indication that you’re able to act more rationally, and not be deceived by that cunning trickster, passion.  I know you’ve recently gone through a breakup, but I hope you can feel how bleak these views can become: to see love only as the window dressing for the propagation of a species, or as just a bridge to the love of wisdom.  This cynicism has other consequences
Wondering if you could redefine love in a relationship with your friend isn’t like a wine-fueled dinner party bouncing around thought experiments

It involves your best friend and his own feelings too, and could risk not only hurting him, but also robbing him of a better romantic partner.  For Simone de Beauvoir, the 20th-century existential philosopher, the most important aspect of life was freedom: We are technically free to do whatever we want, and it’s the choices we make with that freedom that determine our authenticity, or lack of it
De Beauvoir worried about forms of love that stole freedom from other people
In narcissistic love, she wrote in The Second Sex , a partner doesn’t love the other person, but loves the fact that the other loves them
It’s a relationship built on the self-interest of one of its members.  I want to gently point out that it sounds like there may be aspects of the narcissistic relationship in your dilemma
While it may be intriguing to consider what it’s like to date a friend, you don’t seem to be as romantically interested so much as you are interested in his interest in and support of you

Actually involving yourself in such a dynamic could take his freedom, as well as your own capacity to learn from your break-up, then find a partner you’re genuinely drawn to for their own merits.   I’m not saying friendship isn’t an important ingredient in love
Many of the most successful, very long-term partners I know have developed a deep friendship with one another
This friendship helps them stay kind to each other and have fun over many years when work, health, or stress can interrupt more passionate times of connection

title: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan
excerpt: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms Mo
body: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday
Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese
But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”
Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”
The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status

body: Opposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHO An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region

It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries
All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust
